items.title: The Brocken tree limit: treeline, summit syndrome or forest advance?
items.abstract: Climatic treelines mark the low-temperature limit of upright tree growth, yet visible upper tree limits do not necessarily coincide with this thermal boundary. The treeless summit plateau of Mt. Brocken (1,141 m a.s.l.), northern Germany, has repeatedly been interpreted as a climatic treeline. However, visible upper tree limits may also reflect summit syndrome, i.e. exposure-driven suppression of tree stature near mountain summits, as well as historical land use or ongoing management rather than temperature limitation. Here, we reassess the Brocken tree limit using long-term climate records, root-zone temperature measurements, wind data, and recent growth observations of Picea abies. Growing-season temperatures consistently exceeded thermal thresholds commonly associated with global treelines, with mean root-zone temperatures around 8°C in 2025. Growing-season soil temperature well predicted air temperature at the monthly scale, supporting the use of soil temperature measurements as a proxy for thermal conditions at the tree limit: an approach of general utility for logger-based treeline assessment. Long-term air-temperature records likewise remained above commonly reported treeline thresholds and showed significant warming since the 1980s. Spruce individuals surrounding the plateau exhibited vigorous recent height growth, while juvenile trees were observed establishing directly on the plateau. We conclude that the Brocken plateau does not represent a classical temperature-limited treeline but rather an upper tree limit shaped by wind, snow and ice loading and anthropogenic influences (summit syndrome). As such, Mt. Brocken provides a useful model system for distinguishing climatic treelines from exposure- and management-maintained upper tree limits in low-elevation temperate mountains.

items.title: Differential impacts of anthropogenic disturbances on forest structure, diversity, and composition in subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests
items.abstract: Anthropogenic land-use change creates contrasting forest–matrix interfaces, yet comparative evidence of how these interfaces affect forest structure and plant diversity across vegetation strata remains limited. We used a paired-site design comprising 35 sites and 70 plots in a subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest region of central China. Disturbed plots adjacent to Roads, Buildings, Mining, Tourism, and Farming were compared with relatively Undisturbed plots located farther from the corresponding disturbance boundaries. Stand structure and plot-level α-diversity were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with site as a random effect. Community composition was evaluated using paired PERMANOVA, and total Jaccard β-diversity was partitioned into turnover and nestedness-resultant components using paired bootstrap and permutation procedures. Vegetation responses differed among disturbance types and forest layers. Mining reduced stand density, basal area, horizontal and vertical richness, and tree-layer species richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity. Roads increased stand density but reduced basal area, whereas Tourism, Buildings, and Farming reduced stand density. Farming increased herb-layer species richness, while Tourism reduced shrub-layer evenness. Community composition differed between Disturbed and Undisturbed plots in the shrub and herb layers but not in the tree layer. Total Jaccard dissimilarity increased in the tree layer but decreased in the shrub and herb layers. Turnover decreased only in the herb layer, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity did not differ significantly in any layer. These findings demonstrate that vegetation responses at forest-disturbance interfaces are disturbance- and stratum-dependent. Integrating stand structure, α-diversity, community composition, and β-diversity provides a more complete basis for context-specific monitoring and management of adjacent forest remnants than any single indicator alone.

items.title: Synzoochory by scatter-hoarding rodents in a seasonally dry forest of Madagascar
items.abstract: Seed dispersal by scatter-hoarding rodents (synzoochory) is an important mechanism contributing to tree species diversity. Madagascar has a low diversity of frugivorous seed dispersers due to the island’s biogeographical history and lacks native large-bodied terrestrial dispersers. Consequently, relatively small-bodied animals may play important roles as seed dispersers, yet there are limited evaluations of synzoochorous rodents. To address this research gap, we conducted seed-tracking experiments to evaluate the quantitative and qualitative seed dispersal effectiveness of scatter-hoarding rodents in the tropical dry forest of Ankarafantsika National Park, northwestern Madagascar. Our use of a thread-marking method combined with fluorescent paint enabled us to recover more than 93% of removed Anacolosa pervilleana seeds, including those dispersed more than 20 m away. Although two rodent species (Macrotarsomys ingens and Eliurus myoxinus) removed A. pervilleana seeds, M. ingens removed 64.4% of the tagged seeds identified in the video analysis. These rodent species removed 59.1% of placed seeds and dispersed 40.3%; however, only 7.3% of seeds survived for 2 months. The dispersal distances were short (mean = 4.5 m), and most seeds were dispersed within 10 m. Rodents tended to disperse seeds in microhabitats with low understory coverage, where seed survival over the following 2 months was lower than in microhabitats with high understory coverage. These results suggest that scatter-hoarding rodents can serve as seed dispersers, with high quantitative but relatively low qualitative effectiveness. This study highlights the importance of considering rodent-mediated seed dispersal when assessing plant regeneration in Madagascar’s forests.

items.title: Delineating thermal belts in sub-Mediterranean high-mountain Pinus sylvestris forests: the indicator role of understory vegetation
items.abstract: We numerically analysed the floristic composition of Pinus sylvestris forests along an elevational gradient to identify plant community types based on diagnostic species and their role as indicators of thermal belts. We focused our study on the Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) forests of the Guadarrama mountains (Spanish Central System), where two distinct Pinus sylvestris associations have been previously described. Fifty-three plots were sampled covering an altitudinal gradient between 1,410 and 2,080 m. Cluster analysis revealed two elevational belts of pine forests distinguished by the diagnostic, constant and dominant plant species within their understorey. The lower-elevation Pinus sylvestris forests (1,410-1,850 m) were characterized by a temperate element (e.g., Pteridium aquilinum, Galium rotundifolium) and exhibited higher alpha, beta and gamma diversity than the higher-elevation Scots pine forests (1,710-2,080 m), which in turn were defined by an orophilous element (e.g., Juniperus communis subsp. alpina and Jasione laevis). Redundancy analysis showed that Positive Temperature (Tp), a bioclimatic index used to identify thermal belts in the region, was the main climatic factor differentiating the two forest types. Welch’s t-test confirmed significant differences in both understorey alpha diversity and Tp between communities, while plot distribution revealed a transitional threshold at approximately 850. This work highlights the importance of understorey diagnostic species as indicators of bioclimatic belts. Moreover, the higher-elevation Pinus sylvestris forest may constitute a critical sentinel plant community. Monitoring long-term changes in its orophilous understorey could serve as an early-warning indicator of regional climate variation at the southern edge of the species’ distribution area, where these populations are highly vulnerable.

items.title: Priority effects outweigh allelopathy as drivers of potential invasion by absinthe (Artemisia absinthium)
items.abstract: Absinthe wormwood (Artemisia absinthium) is an invasive species that poses significant challenges in both seeded and natural grasslands. One of the hypothesized mechanisms leading to absinthe invasion is allelopathy, in which chemicals produced by absinthe inhibit the growth of other plants. Such allelopathy may be even more important when absinthe establishes prior to other species, leading to chemically induced priority effects. To test how allelopathy and priority effects mediate absinthe competitive effects on four other species commonly found with absinthe, we conducted a greenhouse experiment with three different priority treatments (8 weeks, 4 weeks, and no priority advantage), which we crossed with activated carbon to suppress allelochemicals. Allelopathy improved absinthe growth only when planted simultaneous with other species, but did not affect any other species. Priority gave absinthe a significant competitive advantage, suppressing the growth of other species, although the legume Medicago sativa was less suppressed the longer the priority effect for absinthe. Allelopathy is thus unlikely to be a major driver of initial absinthe invasion, although chemical inhibition may be more important later during the invasion process. Variability among competing species, however, suggests that absinthe may play a major role in structuring plant communities.

items.title: Smoke as an environmental chemical filter for seedling traits of ground-layer Cerrado species
items.abstract: Although smoke water (SW) stimulates germination across fire-prone ecosystems, its effects on Neotropical savannas are still unclear. In the Cerrado, germination patterns are highly species-specific, while seedling traits have been less addressed. Therefore, we currently have a limited understanding of SW effects at different plant life stages. We evaluated the effects of SW concentrations of 10 mL L⁻¹ and 25 mL L⁻¹ (SW1% and SW2.5%, respectively) on seedling growth (shoot length, root length, and root: shoot ratio) of six ground-layer Cerrado species. Seeds were exposed to the different SW concentrations for 60 days, and root and shoot length of the resulting seedlings were measured at the end of the experiment. Stimulatory effects were observed in either the root or shoot length of three species at the lower SW concentration. In contrast, while no inhibitory effects were detected for shoot length, the higher SW concentration inhibited the root length in three species. Concomitantly, this inhibition at SW2.5% led to a lower root: shoot ratio in two of these species. Our results demonstrate that smoke can produce differential effects on seedling growth, acting as an environmental chemical filter that influences the most vulnerable stage of regeneration in post-fire ecosystems.

items.title: Design limitations and ecological evidence constrain conclusions about cattle grazing in Cerrado savannas: a comment on Abreu et al. (2026)
items.abstract: Abreu et al. (2026) propose that cattle grazing may act as a “conservation ally” in Cerrado savannas by reducing fuel loads and partially substituting for fire. We argue that the evidence presented does not support these conclusions. The study relies on a design in which grazing regimes are confounded with site identity and landscape context, limiting causal inference. Reported patterns are more consistent with vegetation degradation than with reversible impacts, including reduced species richness and strong compositional turnover under grazing. In addition, the study is restricted to fire-suppressed conditions that are not representative of Cerrado savannas dynamics, and grazing fails to reduce fuel loads to levels typical of fire-maintained savannas. We suggest that conclusions regarding grazing as a conservation or management tool in Cerrado savannas are premature and should therefore be interpreted more cautiously.

items.title: Contextualizing the effects of cattle in fire-suppressed Cerrado savannas: a response to Cianciaruso and Almeida-Neto (2026)
items.abstract: The commentators critiqued the pseudoreplicated design of the study, interpreted the floristic shifts as irreversible degradation, and argued against our reliance on a fire-suppressed baseline. We counter that while our experimental design has acknowledged statistical limitations, it leverages an exceptionally rare opportunity to evaluate long-term, controlled grazing impacts in adjacent savanna fragments. Contrary to claims of severe degradation, our data demonstrate high ecosystem resilience, marked by rapid structural recovery following short-term cattle exclusion and strong resistance to exotic species invasion. Furthermore, we emphasize that prolonged fire suppression is no longer an “atypical” condition, but the growing socio-ecological reality for fragmented savannas embedded within agricultural matrices, such as mandatory Legal Reserves. Under these specific conditions, cattle grazing significantly reduced hazardous fuel loads by 61%, mitigating catastrophic wildfire risks. Ultimately, we argue that overcoming the institutional taboo against cattle grazing is essential to provide viable economic alternatives for private land conservation in highly threatened Cerrado landscapes.

items.title: Beyond Bactericidal: Plasma Surface Engineering to Defeat Food Matrix-Conditioning Layers.
items.abstract: The persistence of foodborne pathogens on industrial food contact surfaces continues to challenge global food safety despite advances in sanitation technologies. A central limitation of current antimicrobial strategies lies in their validation under simplified laboratory conditions that overlook the physicochemically driven formation of food matrix conditioning films. Upon contact with food residues, organic macromolecules reorganize at the solid‒liquid interface, forming conditioning layers that mask engineered surface functionalities and facilitate microbial attachment. This review examines how such interfacial transformations constrain conventional bactericidal approaches and contribute to sanitization failures in industrial environments. Plasma surface engineering is evaluated as a matrix-aware strategy capable of tailoring surface energy, hydration behavior, and nanoscale architecture through plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition and magnetron sputtering. These approaches may mitigate organic fouling and modulate bacterial surface sensing under controlled conditions. Particular attention is given to mechanotransduction pathways implicated in early biofilm formation, highlighting how nanoscale surface cues influence c-di-GMP signaling and biofilm commitment in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive foodborne pathogens, including Salmonella spp. and Listeria monocytogenes. Significant translational gaps remain, including long-term durability under repeated cleaning-in-place cycles, antimicrobial transport through complex conditioning films, and adaptive tolerance under chronic exposure. This review situates plasma surface engineering within a preventive interfacial design framework, offering an evidence-based rationale for the development of food contact materials capable of meeting the durability, safety, and regulatory demands of modern processing environments.

items.title: Differential Effect of Ivermectin on Intestinal Helminths in Multimmate Mouse (Mastomys natalensis).
items.abstract: Mastomys natalensis is a widespread rodent species in sub-Saharan Africa and is increasingly recognised as an important component of food systems in some communities. However, rodents may harbour gastrointestinal helminths with potential implications for animal health, food safety, and zoonotic disease transmission. Information on gastrointestinal helminth infections in M. natalensis and the response of these parasites to anthelmintic treatment is limited. This study investigated the prevalence and diversity of gastrointestinal helminths in M. natalensis and evaluated changes in helminth egg burden following treatment with Ivermectin. A total of 90 adult M. natalensis, comprising 43 males and 47 females, were captured, and their faecal samples were examined for gastrointestinal helminth eggs. Identified helminths were characterised and their prevalence was estimated with 95% confidence intervals. Following baseline assessment, the rodents were allocated to -treated and untreated control groups. Faecal egg counts, expressed as eggs per gram of faecal sample (EPG), were monitored every 14 days over an eight-week period. The change in egg burden was assessed using faecal egg count reduction (FECR). Five gastrointestinal helminth taxa were identified, of which Hymenolepis diminuta was the most prevalent (39%; 95% CI: 29.6-49.3%), followed by Physaloptera spp. (29%; 95% CI: 20.6-39.1%), Rodentolepis nana (12%; 95% CI: 6.8-20.3%), Strongyloides spp. (11%; 95% CI: 6.1-19.1%), and Trichuris spp. (9%; 95% CI: 4.6-16.7%). In the Ivermectin-treated rodents, mean EPG declined substantially across all five helminth taxa between baseline and weeks post-treatment. The highest egg reductions were observed for H. diminuta (96.4%) and Trichuris spp. (96.2%), followed by Strongyloides spp. (90.9%), Physaloptera spp. (85.5%), and R. nana (80.0%). The untreated control group showed comparatively little change in overall helminth egg burden. Sex-specific analyses showed substantial reductions in both males and females over the same period, except for, R. nana females, where egg counts showed an increase. These findings indicate the potential value of Ivermectin in reducing gastrointestinal helminth egg shedding by M. natalensis. Further studies with larger sample sizes, over a longer period, and appropriate experimental replication are warranted to validate treatment with the anthelminth and its implications for animal health, food safety, and potential zoonotic transmission.

items.title: Probiotic Intervention With Bacillus coagulans and Lactobacillus acidophilus in Small Animals Experimental Ulcerative Colitis: Insights From a Small Animal Model.
items.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is a significant health concern not only in humans but also in companion animals and livestock, where it manifests as chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and mucosal injury. Probiotics have gained increasing attention as potential therapeutic agents due to their immunomodulatory effects and ability to restore intestinal homeostasis. This study investigated the therapeutic efficacy of Bacillus coagulans and Lactobacillus acidophilus in an acetic acid-induced ulcerative colitis model in Wistar rats. Forty male rats were randomly assigned to control, colitis, mesalazine, B. coagulans, and L. acidophilus treatment groups. Disease severity was evaluated by macroscopic and histopathological scoring, colon length and weight, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-1β, IL-17), and inflammasome-associated gene expression (NLRP3, Caspase-1, IL-18, TNF-α). The results showed that colitis induction significantly increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and histological damage compared with controls. Both probiotics markedly reduced inflammatory markers, improved colon morphology, and attenuated inflammasome activation. Their protective effects were comparable to mesalazine, the standard treatment. These findings suggest that B. coagulans and L. acidophilus can serve as effective adjunct therapies for ulcerative colitis in veterinary practice, with potential translational applications for companion animals and livestock.

items.title: A One Health Molecular Investigation and Exploratory Epidemiological Analysis of Cryptosporidium spp. in A Shared Human-Animal Ecosystem.
items.abstract: Introduction Cryptosporidium spp. are enteric protozoan parasites of public health importance, particularly in low-resource settings where humans, animals and environmental water sources frequently interact. This study investigated the prevalence, molecular diversity and environmental exposure-related variables in relation to Cryptosporidium infection in a rural community. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using 180 faecal samples collected from humans, cattle, chickens, fish, cats, dogs, and ducks. Speciation and subtyping were determined through PCR amplification and sequencing of the 18S rRNA and gp60 genes. Epidemiological and environmental data were collected, and univariable analyses were conducted. An exploratory multivariable logistic regression model was subsequently performed for the human subset. Results The overall prevalence of Cryptosporidium infection was 9.40%, with the highest rates observed in humans (14.8%) and cattle (13.5%). Molecular characterisation identified C. hominis, C. parvum, C. bovis and C. felis. Among humans, C. hominis was the predominant, whereas C. parvum was also detected, including mixed infections. gp60 analysis identified multiple subtype families, including Ia, Ib, IIa, IIc and IId. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated close genetic relationships between Bangladeshi isolates and previously reported reference strains from South Asia and the Middle East. Higher odds of Cryptosporidium infection were observed among individuals reporting river bathing and consumption of untreated water, whereas lower odds were observed among those reporting regular handwashing. No statistically significant associations were identified between evaluated environmental variables and infection among non-human hosts. Conclusion The study demonstrated the circulation of multiple Cryptosporidium species and subtype families within a shared human-animal ecosystem. The contaminated surface water and inadequate hygiene practices may represent important environmental exposure interfaces for Cryptosporidium infection in the study area. However, given the cross-sectional design and limited number of positive cases, the epidemiological findings should be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than definitive transmission pathways. Further longitudinal One Health investigations are needed.

items.title: No Trace of Blastocystis Parasite in Bats Caught in the Western and Southwestern Regions of Iran.
items.abstract: Background Blastocystis is a common parasite found in the human intestine, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, and diarrhoea. Bats are potential hosts for this parasite, but little is known about their infection with Blastocystis. Objective Given the diversity of bat species in Iran, this study aimed to investigate Blastocystis infection in bats caught in the southwestern and western regions of the country. Methods Faecal samples were collected from 115 bats from five caves located in Fars, Kurdistan, and Kermanshah provinces. DNA was extracted, using the phenol-chloroform method, and PCR was performed to identify the Blastocystis 18S rRNA gene. Information on bat species was analysed descriptively. Results The four main bat species caught were Miniopterus pallidus (40%, n = 46), Myotis blythii (40%, n = 46), Rhinopoma microphyllum (12.18%, n = 14), and Rhinolophus euryale (7.82%, n = 9). However, none of the 115 stool samples examined showed evidence of Blastocystis infection by the molecular PCR method. Conclusion This study found no evidence of Blastocystis infection in the bat species examined. The unique lifestyle and diet of bats, such as living on cave walls and roofs, may explain this absence. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of bats in the epidemiology of Blastocystis in other regions of Iran.

items.title: Design of Lipopeptides and dsRNA-Lipopeptide Complexes for Sprayable RNAi-Based Plant Protection.
items.abstract: Broad-spectrum insecticides persist in the environment, affecting non-target organisms and selecting for resistant pest populations. In contrast, RNA interference (RNAi) achieves species-targeted pest control triggered by the delivery of exogenous double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which is biodegradable and broken down into harmless components by nucleases. Sprayable applications require suitable formulation strategies for dsRNA protection during delivery. Here, we describe the preparation of dsRNA-lipopeptide complexes (LPCs) composed of non-toxic short-chain lipopeptide surfactants by microfluidic mixing, yielding positively charged dispersions of LPCs < 200 nm in diameter, which encapsulate and protect dsRNA from enzymatic degradation. Some lipopeptides were found to undergo thermo-reversible gelation, self-assembling to fibrillar nanostructures, but remained effective for dsRNA delivery to induce mortality in Colorado potato beetle larvae feeding on sprayed plants. Our results show that lipopeptide surfactants are suitable for the formulation of dsRNA to enable effective delivery to pest insects.

items.title: What health are we talking about? Biodiversity as the missing link between One Health and Planetary Health.
items.abstract: Health has become a central term in global sustainability policy, yet it is often used without sufficient conceptual precision. Public health, global health, One Health, EcoHealth, GeoHealth, and Planetary Health each emphasize different dimensions of the relationship between humans, animals, and the environment. In policy contexts, however, these distinctions are frequently blurred. We argue that biodiversity is often treated as an environmental co-benefit rather than as a foundational determinant of health. This weakens the implementation of One Health approaches because biodiversity underpins disease regulation, immune system development, food and water security, ecosystem functioning, resilience, and climate adaptation. At the same time, biodiversity provides a critical link between One Health and broader Planetary Health challenges, including global environmental change and the transgression of planetary boundaries. Future health and sustainability policies should move beyond generic references to health and explicitly recognize biodiversity as part of preventive health systems.

items.title: Recentering Resource-Based Livelihoods: Prosperity Beyond Extractivism and Pastoralism.
items.abstract: This research note, informed by qualitative fieldwork with resource harvesters in Nova Scotia, explores the effect of economic change and ecological crisis, the outcomes of rural development strategies, and demographic shifts that have shaped the province's rural areas in recent years. It argues that our present moment is ripe with opportunities for a renewed sociological attention on livelihoods in this region, which should take as its focus the relationship that people, communities, and government have with their physical environment. Rural places tend to be valued for their natural endowments, either industrially extracted or preserved and sold as a pastoral idyll. Nova Scotia's recent past has exacerbated this bifurcation. New work is needed to help find prosperous ground beyond both tendencies. This note attempts to spark that effort.

items.title: International qualitative case studies of system-level approaches to promote the development, adoption, and implementation of artificial intelligence in healthcare.
items.abstract: Objectives Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being deployed in health-care settings, yet health systems remain at an early stage in developing approaches to scale effective applications. Much of current activity is characterized by early-stage use cases and pilot projects. In this study, we explored how different health systems are approaching the development, adoption, implementation, and scaling of AI in healthcare to identify transferable lessons for system-level change. Materials and methods We conducted 4 qualitative case studies of health systems and their approaches to scaling AI in healthcare: Catalonia, Norway, Singapore, and Queensland. Data were generated through documents, qualitative interviews and focus groups with strategic decision-makers, policymakers, and lead clinicians. The study explored participants' perspectives on evolving strategies and needs, rationales for change, characteristics of approaches and technologies, expected and experienced benefits, lessons learned, perceived challenges, and elements considered transferable across contexts. Analysis was conducted in 2 stages: an initial within-case thematic analysis, followed by a cross-case analysis informed by the Technology, People, Organization, and Macroenvironment framework, while also allowing inductive themes to emerge. Results The dataset consisted of 60 documents, 34 interviews, and 5 focus groups. We consulted a total of 50 different participants from case study sites across data collection activities. Our findings indicate that AI scaling trajectories in health-care systems are strongly shaped by existing digital strategies, historical and cultural contexts of digitalization, funding arrangements, and legacy technological infrastructures. Approaches to accelerating safe AI adoption at scale were characterized by efforts to orchestrate and coordinate change across multiple stakeholder groups with differing and evolving spheres of influence. Within this context, scaling was shaped by opportunities for experimentation, incentive structures, and the distribution of decision-making authority. Sustained use and wider spread of AI applications can be supported through ongoing post-deployment monitoring and the central collation and dissemination of emerging evidence. Crucially, these activities need to be embedded within a broader ecosystem that foregrounds learning, partnership, governance, and procurement as integral components of scaling. Conclusion Our findings suggest that strategic decision-makers need to move beyond the conventional dichotomy of "top-down" and "bottom-up" approaches to scaling AI and instead conceptualize scaling as a process of multilevel orchestration.

items.title: Nitrogen and Sulfur Assimilation in Fish Otoliths Evaluated by Stable Isotope Labeling and NanoSIMS Analysis.
items.abstract: Rationale Stable nitrogen (δ 15 N) and sulfur (δ 34 S) isotopes within the metabolically inert organic matrix of teleost otoliths provide high-fidelity archives for reconstructing animal life histories. However, low organic content limits the spatial resolution of conventional bulk isotopic analysis, leaving biomineralization kinetics and the temporal integration of these dietary signals poorly quantified. We utilized nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (NanoSIMS) to overcome these limitations and determine intracrystalline isotopic dynamics. Methods Isotopic pulses were established by feeding juvenile Mozambique tilapia (Oreochromis mossambicus) 15 N-enriched algae and diets supplemented with L-methionine- 34 S, utilizing Alizarin Red S fluorescent marking for precise temporal referencing. High-resolution and in situ NanoSIMS analysis was applied to quantify the temporal distribution of the labeling signals within the otolith organic matrix. A first-order kinetic model was used to estimate isotopic dynamics half-lives (t 50% ). Results NanoSIMS analysis revealed rapid isotopic changes across both assimilation and depuration phases (t 50% = 0.5-13.9 days). Both δ 15 N and δ 34 S exhibited statistically indistinguishable kinetics, reflecting synchronized metabolic routing where dietary signals are deposited directly into the otolith without being buffered by internal tissue reserves. Crucially, the dietary matrix modulated assimilation; despite comparable dietary δ 34 S proportions, otolith sulfur incorporation and signal attenuation were significantly faster in fish fed algae-based diets than in those fed eel-meal-based diets. This demonstrates the preferential utilization of exogenous labeled methionine when the base diet is naturally deficient in this essential amino acid. Conclusions High-resolution NanoSIMS profiling demonstrates that the otolith organic matrix archives dietary signals governed by rapid assimilation pathways rather than strict thermodynamic equilibrium. This analytical approach establishes a crucial mechanistic basis and experimental framework for utilizing intracrystalline organic isotopes as precise indicators in trophic ecology.

items.title: Psychoeducational Challenges of Dyslexic Children During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Dyslexic students faced psychological and educational challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic and online learning, including increased anxiety, low self-esteem, reduced reading interest, limited access to educational technologies, insufficient teacher support, and difficulties with reading fluency and concentration. Examining these challenges is crucial for implementing effective measures and enhancing post-pandemic learning. This study investigates the psycho-educational challenges of dyslexic children during the pandemic, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to support them in current and future contexts. This systematic review identified relevant articles through electronic searches of PubMed, Wiley, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by the snowballing technique, which involved examining the bibliographies of retrieved references. The study identified two main categories of challenges for dyslexic children: psychological (mental health, emotional well-being, behavioural issues, parental stress) and educational (socioeconomic status, technology access, special educational needs, teacher support, remote learning difficulties) affecting children with learning disabilities. The research results show that dyslexic children faced various psychological and educational difficulties identified in this review during the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, targeted, evidence-based strategies-such as teacher training, family-school collaboration, adaptive learning technologies, and psychological support-are needed to mitigate these challenges in the post-pandemic period.

items.title: Leopard sterilisation in India: The ecological and ethical costs of anthropocentric wildlife management.
items.abstract: India's rising human-leopard conflict has prompted the government to adopt immune contraceptives to manage leopard populations. The decision has sparked debate among wildlife experts and conservation organisations, government officials, and local communities. Here, I discuss the ecological and ethical implications of this intervention and highlight alternative, coexistence-based approaches that recognise both humans and wildlife as stakeholders within shared socio-ecological systems.

items.title: Do Adverse Intrauterine Environments Affect Body Mass Index in Infants and Preschool Children?
items.abstract: Exposure to adverse intrauterine environments resulting from different maternal clinical conditions may alter childhood growth patterns. This study investigated the influence of such environments on body mass index-for-age (BMI-for-age) trajectories from birth to preschool age. A total of 342 mother-child dyads recruited from three hospitals in southern Brazil were allocated into five groups: diabetes mellitus (DM), systemic arterial hypertension (SAH), maternal smoking, small for gestational age (SGA, used here as a proxy for impaired fetal growth), and a control group. Children were assessed at seven time points from birth to preschool age using anthropometric measurements to calculate BMI-for-age z-scores. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) identified a significant interaction between group and time (p < 0.001). Among girls, at birth, the DM group presented higher BMI-for-age z-scores than the smoking group and reached elevated BMI-for-age z-scores at preschool age, differing from the control group. At 6 months of age, girls in the SGA group showed a marked increase in BMI-for-age. Among boys, the SGA group reached higher BMI-for-age values at preschool age than the DM and control groups. Differences were observed across time, group, and sex in the SGA and control groups (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that adverse intrauterine environments may influence BMI-for-age trajectories during early life, with greater variability and evidence of catch-up growth among children exposed to maternal DM and SGA. Results should be interpreted cautiously due to unequal subgroup sizes and substantial loss to follow-up at preschool age.

items.title: Capturing Thought Dynamics: Modeling the Structure of Spontaneous Associations.
items.abstract: Human thought unfolds in patterns that vary across individuals; some move fluidly across ideas, whereas others return to narrower or more repetitive paths. Here, we asked whether structural aspects of associative thinking-its breadth, trajectory, and temporal pace-can account for individual differences in repetitive thought styles such as rumination. Participants completed brief free-association tasks, and their responses were quantified using a model trained on large-scale free association data to derive individual structural profiles of associative flow. Across two independent samples, these profiles predicted self-reported measures of rumination and repetitive thinking, with nonlinear models accounting for meaningful inter-individual variation and showing generalization across tasks and datasets. These findings suggest that individual differences in repetitive thought are reflected not only in what people think about but also in how associations are organized and unfold over time. Structural modeling therefore provides a viable approach to characterizing spontaneous cognition through patterns of associative organization.

items.title: Ecological Momentary Assessments of Daily Pain Experiences in Bothersome and High-Impact Chronic Pain.
items.abstract: Background High-impact chronic pain (HICP), defined as persistent pain substantially limiting daily activities, affects millions of adults and poses a public health challenge. However, as prior knowledge comes largely from retrospective self-report measures, little is known about how HICP manifests in daily life. Methods This study used the comprehensive Ecological Momentary Assessment of pain (cEMAp) instrument to assess pain-related experiences four times daily over 7 days in individuals with chronic musculoskeletal pain. Using the Graded Chronic Pain Scale-Revised, we compared individuals with HICP (n = 66) with bothersome chronic pain (n = 41), a group with similar pain frequency but less interference with daily activities. Each prompt assessed pain intensity, interference, cognitions, behaviours, coping strategies, and pain characteristics over the preceding 2 h. Results Both groups reported similar pain intensity levels, but the HICP group reported more frequent interference with physical, mental, and social activities. No group differences emerged in daily mood or negative pain-related cognitions. Exploratory analyses suggested that many daily experiences were similar across groups, with differences observed in selected pain qualities, coping strategies, and pain behaviours. Analyses of response distributions showed some similarity across groups in many experiences. Conclusions The most consistent distinction between the groups was interference frequency, consistent with the operationalization of HICP as pain that disrupts daily functioning, while several other pain-related experiences were similar across groups. cEMAp data complement traditional retrospective assessment by providing a more detailed view of biopsychosocial aspects of chronic pain in everyday life. Significance statement Prior understanding of high-impact chronic pain (HICP) has largely relied on retrospective measures. Using the comprehensive Ecological Momentary Assessment of pain (cEMAp) instrument, we found that HICP was distinguished primarily by more frequent interference with daily activities rather than greater pain intensity. Our findings also reveal similarities and differences across other pain-related experiences, highlighting the value of multidimensional real-world assessment beyond pain intensity alone.

items.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
items.abstract: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these "strength-based organizational approaches" and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees' broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants' likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees' equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees' lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors' positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person-context interactions. items.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
items.abstract: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens ("in" or "on") but rather as objects' properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
items.abstract: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: The orthographic mind: Orthographic imagery propensity correlates with semantic structure and sensory sensitivity.
items.abstract: Individuals differ in their habitual use of internal representational modes, including visual imagery, internal verbalization, and orthographic imagery (the mental simulation of written word forms). The present research examined whether such internal representational propensities relate to semantic organization and external information engagement. Across two studies (total N = 1,399), we assessed individuals' internal representational modes using the Internal Representations Questionnaire and examined their associations with semantic structure (nine-word semantic rating experiments; N = 1,109) and external information engagement (sensory-processing sensitivity and mobile app usage). Orthographic imagery showed robust associations with both semantic geometry and external information engagement patterns: Individuals with stronger orthographic imagery showed greater cross-category semantic association strength, lower semantic conformity, and lower sensory-processing sensitivity. Internal verbalization was positively associated with within-category semantic cohesion, while visual imagery showed no reliable associations with semantic geometry and limited associations with real-world media engagement. Effects were modest but consistent across experiments. These findings suggest that internal representational modes function as stable weighting biases, subtly modulating semantic geometry and sensory-processing profiles. Such propensities therefore correspond to structured variations in cognition, rather than merely phenomenological differences in inner experience. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
items.abstract: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5-6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5-6 and 8-9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor's color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5-6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices.
items.abstract: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in "master virtues" that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a "master virtue." However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful "master vices." These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people's beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
items.abstract: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people's memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition-a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative-but not item-memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Correction to "Systematically reducing schematic information during encoding differentially impacts true and false memory at retrieval in younger and older adults" by Becker et al. (2026).
items.abstract: Reports an error in "Systematically reducing schematic information during encoding differentially impacts true and false memory at retrieval in younger and older adults" by Alexa Becker, Rebecca L. Wagner and Nancy A. Dennis ( Psychology and Aging , Advanced Online Publication, Jul 23, 2026, np; see record 2028-01807-001). Jordan Chamberlain was missing from the author list in the submitted manuscript. The authorship has been corrected with the agreement of all authors. All versions of this article have been corrected. (The following abstract of the original article appeared in record 2028-01807-001.) Schemas are abstract representations that aid memory performance by providing a structured context through which memories can be both encoded and retrieved. Older adults have been shown to particularly benefit from schema support as a memory aid. Yet, while helpful to true memory for schematic information, reliance on schemas has also been shown to lead to high rates of false memories for novel yet schematically related information, as well as diminished memory for information that falls outside of an active schema. The current research sought to examine how systematically manipulating naturalistic contextualization as well as the density of schematic information present during encoding may alter subsequent true and false memory for both schematic and nonschematic information. To examine this, we systematically altered the ratio of schematic-to-nonschematic information present during encoding across four conditions in a sample of healthy younger and older adults. Overall, both younger and older adults responded more accurately to schematic compared to nonschematic targets, replicating past work highlighting the benefit of schemas to memory performance. Results also showed that systematically reducing the amount of schematic information present at encoding improved memory discriminability. Specifically, as there was less schematic information present at encoding, false alarms to schematic lures decreased, and hits to nonschematic targets increased. Additionally, when items were decontextualized from a naturalistic scene, false alarms to nonschematic lures decreased. Hits to schematic targets were equitable across conditions. Taken together, the results demonstrate that while schemas maintain a strong influence on memory performance across the lifespan, this effect can be manipulated with reduced schematic information. Such findings reveal the extent to which the pervasive influence of schemas on memory can be swayed by manipulating the amount of schematic information present during encoding and provide critical knowledge for the optimal usage of schemas as a memory support across the lifespan. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Different object features shape mnemonic discrimination in younger and older adults.
items.abstract: The ability to discriminate experiences in memory is an important indicator of cognitive health in older age and a sensitive marker of hippocampal integrity. Measures of mnemonic discrimination, such as the mnemonic similarity task, have the potential to become early diagnostic tools of Alzheimer's dementia. It is thus important to understand how hippocampus-dependent memory functions interact with nonmnemonic processes to determine mnemonic discrimination performance. In this study, we investigate which features contribute to mnemonic discrimination in younger and older age. First, we found in a sample of younger (n = 93, 20-30 years) and older adults (n = 103, 65-82 years) that age impacted performance on the mnemonic similarity task above and beyond the effect of perceptual discrimination of novel 2D configurative objects. Next, in two experiments, we acquired similarity and feature difference ratings for the mnemonic similarity task lures from younger (n = 25 and n = 47, 19-37 years) and older (n = 25 and n = 47, 65-79 years) adults. Using random forest regression and representational similarity analysis, we found that the two groups exhibited unique similarity rating patterns. Finally, enriching our memory data with the feature information, we showed, on the trial level, that mnemonic decisions of older and younger adults are affected by distinct object features. Altogether, these results provide evidence that older adults perceive the differences in lure images distinctively and they may rely on different levels of representations for mnemonic discrimination. items.title: Age-related changes in memory for gist and details: New perspectives on the representational quality of episodic memory.
items.abstract: Substantial heterogeneity in adult age-related declines in episodic memory within and across tasks and individuals has prompted extensive theoretical debate about the source of these variations. Today, many theories assume that age-related changes in the representational fidelity of memory and the degree to which a test demands the retrieval of specific details of past experiences underlie much of this variability. This special issue of Psychology and Aging presents 19 contributions from researchers from around the world that together aim to enrich our understanding of the representational basis of age-related memory change. These contributions explore several interrelated themes related to measuring, predicting, and, at times, counteracting age-related declines in memory specificity while extending representational accounts to new tasks, more naturalistic contexts, and populations spanning the adult lifespan as well as individuals with neurocognitive impairment. The breadth of coverage spans multiple research domains with rich histories in the field of cognitive aging, including recognition memory, autobiographical memory, event memory, decision making, comprehension, and computational modeling. Collectively, the diversity of questions posed by the articles and the varied methods they advance to addressing them highlight the value of integrating findings across different research traditions to develop a more unified framework for studying age-related changes in memory specificity. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: An open-source standardized pipeline for equitable observations of interactive behavioral dynamics: Theory-driven measurement, analysis, and masking.
items.abstract: Behavioral observation has a long-standing tradition in psychology. However, its reliance on manual coding makes observational methods costly and prone to biases that arise from the inherent limits of coding schemes and from the subjectivity of human raters. Behavioral observation research therefore has drawbacks in terms of applicability, accessibility, reproducibility, and equitability. Computer vision (CV) methods have promise in this regard. In the context of quantifying human movement, CV approaches to pose estimation are becoming increasingly precise and have the benefit of being nonintrusive, reproducible, and low cost. With such methods, human movement in videos can be processed as multivariate time-series data, offering a basis for a more comprehensive analysis of individual, interpersonal, and social dynamics, opening up the possibility for the widespread study of diverse populations in out-of-lab real-world contexts. Fulfilling such a promise goes beyond technical progress, it requires a theory-driven implementation of new accessible observational methods made equitable to learn. To showcase this promise, we present a CV pipeline with analyses of the temporal dynamics of dyadic interactions, including a cross-cultural investigation of movement fluidity in sibling cooperation during task-focused interactions and longitudinal assessments of infant-caregiver coordination during free-play sessions. The pipeline incorporates a pedagogical computational notebook, pose estimation (YOLOv8), theory-driven linear and nonlinear time-series analysis, and a CV method for more privacy-aware video data archiving. Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it. items.title: Building the Etch-a-Sketch online (ESO) system to broaden and diversify research: Proof of concept for a tool to automate sentiment coding of transcripts from online parent-child observations.
items.abstract: Parent-child relationships are mutually reinforcing dynamics associated with children's psychological adjustment across races and cultures. Observing and rating (coding) naturalistic parent-child interactions is central to understanding psychological mechanisms, targeting interventions, and measuring change, yet pragmatic barriers to in-person assessment (e.g., time, travel, cost) limit their use in large, diverse samples. The online observation tool, Etch-a-Sketch Online (ESO), enables developmentally, racially, and culturally flexible data collection, but human coding of ESO interactions remains resource intensive. This proof-of-concept study introduces SwiftSentiment, an open-access, cost-free, data-secure artificial intelligence-powered tool for sentiment analysis (i.e., identifying emotional tone from text) of ESO-elicited conversations. The sample comprised 62 mothers and fathers recruited in the United Kingdom with their children (46.67% female; Mage = 13.17 years [SD = 1.32], 64.52% White, 20.97% Asian/British Asian, 14.52% mixed/other ethnicity). Associations between human coding of ESO interaction videos (using the established parent-child interaction system) and SwiftSentiment coding of the interactions' audio transcripts were examined, as were human and SwiftSentiment coding associations with self-reported parent-child relationships and child adjustment. Correlations between broad-coded SwiftSentiment emotional positivity and negativity from audio transcripts and human-coded parent-child positivity and negativity from video demonstrated convergent validity of SwiftSentiment coding. SwiftSentiment negativity was associated with self-reported dysfunctional parenting strategies and child externalizing problems, but unlike manual coding, SwiftSentiment positivity was not associated with parent-reported constructs, suggesting that human coding retains advantages in capturing positivity. The study provides initial evidence for partnering ESO and SwiftSentiment as an innovative data collection and automated coding system-the ESO system-to widen and diversify research capacity and reach. items.title: Toward equitable fidelity measurement of evidence-based psychosocial interventions.
items.abstract: Accurately measuring clinician fidelity to psychosocial evidence-based interventions (EBIs) is essential to advance equitable EBI implementation. Observational measures of live or recorded therapy sessions are widely considered the most reliable and valid metrics for indexing fidelity. However, they are costly, time and resource intensive, and rarely used in underresourced clinical settings; this makes it challenging to assess the quality of care delivered to underserved populations. Further, many fidelity coding schemes originated from clinical trials testing relatively structured clinical protocols with primarily White, middle-class individuals. This raises equity considerations for their use and interpretation in settings serving individuals with diverse identities and adverse social determinants of health, where flexible EBI application is often required to meet needs. For example, fidelity coding schemes do not always consider patient cultural and contextual factors that may lead clinicians to "stray" from fidelity standards. Guided by the health equity implementation framework, we outline key equity considerations related to observational fidelity measurement and interpretation in mental health. We describe several ongoing efforts to equitably assess fidelity to psychosocial EBIs in underresourced community settings using a variety of strategies including standardized patient paradigms codeveloped with community partners, snapshot coding of session recordings, artificial intelligence models that automate fidelity score generations, and leveraging expert consultation encounters to generate actionable fidelity data. We conclude by discussing implications for future research. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Developmental engaged methods of observation (DEMO): A proposal for science and society.
items.abstract: Observational research that involves observers from the communities and contexts researchers aim to study can make research more valid while representing community views and interests. Developmental science is a key area where community-engaged approaches can make valuable contributions, especially considering the challenges inherent in observing children and families. This conceptual article proposes an approach for effectively gathering observational data while enhancing equity in science: Developmental Engaged Methods of Observation. This approach brings together insights from developmental science, participatory science research (which involves training community members to serve as data collectors who observe the world around them), and participatory action research (which centers the voices of the communities that are being studied). This article illustrates what the approach can look like by discussing several case studies from contemporary developmental research in families, schools, and everyday settings on topics like human development, academic integrity, and science identity. The Developmental Engaged Methods of Observation approach forwards new ways of thinking about developmental observation research that can bolster diversity in science, create new insight into developmental processes and mechanisms across contexts, and create opportunities for trust and partnership with stakeholders across a range of communities. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Taking a bottom-up, data-driven approach to characterizing variability across early-life environments.
items.abstract: Children's long-term outcomes correlate with the physical and social features of the homes, schools, and neighborhoods in which they grow up. Yet, current techniques for establishing these correlations are limited. This article (a) presents five main issues linked to the currently used approaches. For example, most research relies on questionnaires or coding brief videoed interactions, which focus on a limited set of dimensions selected by researchers ("top-down" approach). As a result, these methods are limited because they provide only a static snapshot, which often conflates conceptually diverse levels, including the physical (e.g., noise, light) and social environments (e.g., caregiver mood, responsiveness). New technologies offer alternative approaches to these issues. This article (b) highlights how continuous multifeature observations, processed using machine learning tools, can improve our description of early development and inform theorizing of the mechanisms through which environments shape outcomes. Devices worn by children and those around them provide long-form recordings, allowing researchers to track how naturalistic environments vary over time and how children respond to them in real time. This shift supports a more dynamic, bottom-up, data-driven, and potentially culturally neutral approach to characterizing environmental variability. Finally, the article (c) discusses key limitations, notably the need to ensure that machine learning methods used to analyze early environments are trained using culturally diverse data, evaluating remaining risks of bias, and practical and ethical considerations. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Feasibility and equity in the assessment of parent-child interactions: Lessons from three approaches.
items.abstract: Observations of parent-child interactions provide critical insights that directly inform developmental theory and treatment initiatives. Equitable and feasible assessment is necessary to fully understand the spectrum of relevant parent and child behaviors accounting for cultural, ethnic, racial, and linguistic diversity. Parent-child observational research has primarily relied on structured, in-person recordings later coded by research assistants. This approach introduces logistical barriers for families coming into the laboratory, significant time and labor cost for coding, and potential limitations in ecological validity. With the advent and application of new, agile approaches for parent-child behavioral observation and coding, it is critical to evaluate which methods may improve feasibility, accessibility of participation, diverse representation, and ecological validity. This article examines the strengths and limitations of three innovative observational methodologies to assess parent-child interactions among ethnically, linguistically, and geographically diverse families: (a) structured male-caregiver-child interactions via videoconferencing with live coding (N = 114), (b) recording speech in naturalistic parent-child interactions via smartphone application with AI-supported coding (N = 27), and (c) naturalistic interactions in the home via wearable video-recording device (N = 27). A detailed discussion is provided focused on the (a) feasibility, utility, and cost of these methods, (b) clinical implications, (c) ability to overcome logistical barriers and promote equitable access to diverse families, (d) and ethical implications of standard, AI-supported, and live coding methods. Implications of this work contribute to understanding how to improve equity in the assessment of parent-child interactions, as well as increase the feasibility of behavioral observation for researchers. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Applying observational methods to antiracist research with White families.
items.abstract: In an effort to disrupt ongoing racial injustice, many areas of psychology are increasingly interrogating Whiteness-defined as a system of cultural practices, laws, and institutions that confer privilege and resources to White individuals. Features of Whiteness, including avoidance, defensiveness, and self-presentation bias, present unique methodological challenges that render observational methods indispensable for antiracist research with White participants and families. This article outlines innovative approaches to manage the influence of Whiteness and racism on research teams and observational methodologies, tailor methods to both parents' and children's developmental levels, and incorporate technology to expand observations beyond the lab. In particular, we focus on the use of observational methods to study White racial socialization, a key mechanism through which racism or antiracism is conveyed across generations. Our recommendations are illustrated through practical and empirical lessons from a case study of The CARPE DIEM Study, which evaluates a novel antiracist parenting intervention for White mothers of White children. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Methodological innovations for advancing equitable observations of human behavior and social interactions in psychological science.
items.abstract: The purpose of this special issue was to bring together articles discussing pragmatic, new, equitably informed methodologies for the use of behavioral observation in psychology. This introduction highlights main themes that emerged across the published articles, such as the importance of theory and innovative methods in observational research, the use of artificial intelligence in observational coding and data collection, and methods that advance equitable observation principles. Articles highlight strategies and tips for the use of observational methods that are more pragmatic, less costly, and less time intensive. Additionally, articles discuss the use of observational methods across settings (e.g., home, school, and therapeutic), modalities (e.g., wearables, virtual), and analytic methods (e.g., machine learning). We conclude the introduction with ethical considerations that emerged across the special issue, as well as the need for the use of pragmatic observational methods in large, epidemiological studies. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Investigating Interoceptive Beliefs in Individuals With Endometriosis.
items.abstract: Background Research has indicated that individuals experiencing chronic pain differ in their ability to sense and interpret signals arising from inside the body, termed interoception. It is unclear whether differences in interoception exist for those with endometriosis, a common condition where pain is a major symptom. Methods This study aimed to investigate whether interoceptive beliefs are altered in individuals with a diagnosis of endometriosis compared to those without, and whether pain experienced by those with endometriosis predicted interoceptive beliefs. Interoceptive beliefs were assessed in 247 participants with endometriosis and 98 participants without the condition. Those with endometriosis also reported their experience of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and chronic pelvic pain. Results Individuals with endometriosis reported that they noticed more internal signals but had reduced trust in these signals and were more worried by them. They also reported that they try to distract themselves from internal sensations more than those without endometriosis. Increased pain intensity predicted higher scores in one facet of interoceptive beliefs, such that higher levels of pain were associated with higher awareness of internal sensations in individuals with endometriosis. Conclusions These results indicate that those with endometriosis differ in their interoceptive beliefs and that these differences may be influenced by their pain experience. Given these findings largely align with changes observed in other conditions marked by pain, it is possible that interoceptive changes may represent a transdiagnostic characteristic across individuals experiencing pain. Significance This study addresses previously conflicted findings in the literature, providing a clearer picture of the changes in interoceptive beliefs present in people with endometriosis. Developing a stronger understanding of interoceptive functioning in this unique population may lead to opportunities to develop stronger interventions targeting bodily sensations in pain management in those with the condition.

items.title: Time Flows With the Changing of Events.
items.abstract: In recent years, investigations into the psychological experience of time have rapidly accelerated. The experience of time could depend on a ticking internal clock or rely on contextual changes within and between events. Cognitive theories of memory propose that the presence of event boundaries, as defined by unexpected changes, is crucial for the segmentation of sequenced content and ultimately, the formation of long-term memories. Interestingly, the experience of change also influences the temporal distances between memories. Concurrent lines of research have developed similar theories on the experience of time, with salient contextual changes distorting temporal experience. Herein, we propose a unification of theories from the fields of time and memory. Events are creatively constructed and encoded into long-term memory if sufficient changes occur. The subjective experience of time is also determined by an accumulation of changes creating temporal distances between memories. The encoding of memories provides temporal tags at multiple nested timescales, with no need to synchronize with the relative number of seconds that have passed, and duration estimates require a reconstruction of information between anchor points. Time does not exist without change, and experiencing change is fundamental for the formation of lasting memories.

items.title: GABAergic Network Dysregulation in Alcohol Use Disorder: Receptor-Transporter Interactions Driving the Transition From Goal-Directed to Compulsive Behaviour.
items.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is characterized by a shift from controlled, goal-directed drinking to compulsive, habitual alcohol (a.k.a. ethanol) seeking, even in the face of negative outcomes. This transition is closely associated with alterations in cortico-striatal circuitry and dysregulated GABAergic signalling, both of which drive the progression from flexible control to compulsive behaviour. Acute alcohol exposure enhances GABAergic inhibition, primarily by increasing presynaptic GABA release. Chronic exposure leads to compensatory neuroadaptations, such as subunit reorganization, receptor internalization and diminished GABA receptor sensitivity. While these neuroadaptations alter receptor-mediated GABAergic signalling during dependence and withdrawal, they also alter dopaminergic regulation and further reinforce alcohol-seeking behaviour. Beyond receptor-level adaptations, impaired GABA clearance, especially through the astrocytic transporter GAT3, plays a crucial role in regulating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition. This effect is particularly evident within the dorsal striatum, where elevated tonic GABA shifts control from flexible, goal-directed action towards rigid, habitual responding by altering the balance between the dorsomedial and dorsolateral subregions. Consistent with these mechanistic insights, animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behaviour, reinforcing impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioural shift. Taken together, these lines of evidence validate a central therapeutic model, namely, that targeting altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance in AUD could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains the disorder. Overall, this work supports a unifying model in which receptor adaptations and disrupted GABA removal maintain altered inhibitory tone, driving maladaptive circuit function and contributing to the persistence of AUD.
