items.title: Evaluation of stream habitat suitability using the HMUs clustering method and habitat diversity index
items.abstract: Abstract The objectives of this study were to classify streamflow patterns into Hydro-Morphological Units (HMUs) using hydrodynamic factors and to evaluate stream habitats based on these HMU clusters. A 2.9 km reach of the Bokha stream was selected as the study area, where aquatic habitat enhancement is required. Stream velocity and water depth were simulated using the HEC-RAS 2D model. Based on the simulation results, the stream flow patterns were categorized into five HMU types—pools, riffles, rapids, ruffles, and runs—according to estimated probabilities derived from their respective hydrodynamic boundary ranges. Spatiotemporal analysis indicated that HMUs such as ruffle and run closely corresponded with observed fish habitat characteristics, suggesting their suitability as indicators for habitat evaluation. To quantitatively assess habitat diversity, the Normalized Shannon–Weaver Index was calculated, yielding values of 0.93 at the minimum ecological streamflow (0.48 m³/s) and 0.88 at the maximum Weighted Usable Area (WUA) flow (6.9 m³/s). Overall, the proposed approach provides a robust framework for stream habitat evaluation and contributes to the identification of streamflow ranges that are both ecologically meaningful and practically feasible, thereby supporting sustainable stream management strategies.

items.title: A lifetime in conservation: an interview with Chris Dickman on biodiversity loss, introduced species, and ways forward
items.abstract: This paper presents an interview with Australian conservation scientist Chris Dickman, conducted in December 2025 as part of a broader inquiry into conservation and introduced species. The inquiry explored areas of both agreement and disagreement among 16 conservation scientists and practitioners, with the aim of identifying ways to work productively across differing perspectives in pursuit of better conservation outcomes. This paper presents only the interview with Chris, and rather than presenting a formal academic argument, it retains Chris’s personal voice and reflections on a lifetime of conservation research and practice. The interview foregrounds Chris’s personal reflections and way of thinking, and accumulated experience. It explores the experiences that shaped his views on biodiversity loss, introduced species, nativeness, and conservation policy. Across these topics, Chris combines deep concern for Australia’s declining biodiversity with a scientific curiosity that resists simple solutions. He reflects on the limitations of broadscale culling programs, the importance of evaluating conservation success through outcomes for native species, the ecological value of dingoes, and the need to explore a wider range of humane management approaches, including habitat restoration, genetic resilience, and emerging tools such as chemical camouflage. A key issue identified is the lack of public awareness about the biodiversity crisis among the Australian public and helping people develop stronger relationships with Australia’s unique environment. The interview offers insight into a conservation perspective characterised by scientific rigour, humility, adaptability, and respect for differing viewpoints while maintaining an unwavering commitment to preventing further extinctions.

items.title: INTEGRATIVE MULTI‑MARKER BARCODING AND ITS PHYLOGENY RESOLVE VIETNAMESE STRAIN CCAH013/2 AS Mychonastes rotundus (Sphaeropleales, Chlorophyceae)
items.abstract: A coccoid green microalga (strain CCAH013/2) isolated from a mangrove edge freshwater site in Can Gio, Viet Nam was identified through an integrative workflow combining morphology with multi marker DNA evidence. Nuclear 18S rRNA and plastid 23S rRNA sequences showed very high similarity to named Mychonastes taxa, supporting placement at the genus level but offering limited interspecific resolution due to locus conservatism. The ITS region (ITS1–5.8S–ITS2) provided species level power: BLAST results reached ≥ 99% identity to Mychonastes rotundus and dropped markedly for other congeners (≤~ 95%). A maximum likelihood tree inferred from ITS recovered CCAH013/2 within the M. rotundus clade with strong bootstrap support, mirroring the pairwise identity pattern. Morphological characters-small, spherical to slightly oval, non motile cells occurring in minute clusters and reproducing by autospores-were congruent with the emended generic concept and the species diagnosis. Together, these data support a robust assignment of CCAH013/2 to Mychonastes rotundus and provide a basis for applied studies under local conditions, including CO₂ enrichment tolerance, lipid and carotenoid productivity, and small scale pilot tests in tropical coastal freshwater niches.

items.title: Protecting the Greater One-Horned Rhinoceros: The Role of Workforce Capacity, Legal Enforcement, and Patrolling in Protected Areas
items.abstract: This study examines the relationship between anti-poaching management strategies and wild greater one-horned rhinoceros population outcomes in Assam, India. Drawing on archival data from the Assam Forest Department, the study assesses whether key anti-poaching measures, including frontline staffing levels, personnel salary expenditures, poacher arrests, and patrolling efforts, are associated with changes in wild rhino populations. The findings reveal that frontline staffing levels and salary expenditures are significantly associated with rhinoceros population recovery, suggesting that investments in human resources may strengthen deterrence, field monitoring, and habitat protection. Legal enforcement, measured by the number of poachers arrested, also demonstrates a statistically significant association with rhinoceros population outcomes, highlighting the importance of effective law enforcement in anti-poaching strategies. In contrast, patrolling effort alone was not a statistically significant predictor of rhinoceros population changes, suggesting that patrol effectiveness may depend on complementary measures, such as adequate staffing, consistent law enforcement, and systematic monitoring. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of institutional capacity and coordinated enforcement strategies in rhinoceros conservation. The study offers practical policy implications for prioritizing investments in frontline personnel, strengthening enforcement capacity, and improving monitoring systems to support long-term rhinoceros population recovery.

items.title: Mycorrhizal Networks
items.abstract: Introduction and Definition: Mycorrhizae are widespread symbiotic associations between fungi and plant roots that extend fungal access into the surrounding soil. The term mycorrhiza describes this close relationship: “A mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus and the roots of a vascular plant.” When mycorrhizal fungal mycelium associates with the roots of multiple plants, it can form a common mycorrhizal network (CMN). Mycorrhizal associations play fundamental roles in terrestrial ecosystems by contributing to nutrient cycling, soil stability, plant growth, and ecosystem resilience. Mycorrhizal symbioses are estimated to have originated approximately 400–450 million years ago, contributing to the colonization of land by early plants.Body: Major forms of mycorrhizal associations include arbuscular, ectomycorrhizal, ericoid, and orchid mycorrhizae, which differ in their fungal partners, structures, and host ranges. In these associations, plants provide photosynthetically derived carbon to fungi, while fungi enhance plant access to water and mineral nutrients. Mycorrhizal associations influence ecosystem functioning by enhancing nutrient acquisition, supporting soil aggregation, and affecting plant community composition and soil carbon cycling. Common mycorrhizal networks have been investigated as potential pathways for the movement of resources and signals among associated plants. Experimental studies have detected movement of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus among plants associated with common fungal mycelia, as well as defence-associated responses in connected plants. However, the magnitude, mechanisms, and ecological consequences of these processes vary among experimental systems and remain under investigation. Knowledge of mycorrhizal symbioses is informing research in sustainable agriculture, forestry, reforestation, and ecosystem restoration. Recent scientific debate has emphasized the importance of distinguishing evidence that plants are connected, evidence that resources or signals move between them, and evidence that these processes provide ecologically meaningful benefits to recipient plants. This distinction is central to ongoing research into the ecological significance of common mycorrhizal networks.

items.title: From conflicts to coexistence between people and wildlife – coverage by European Journal of Wildlife Research
items.abstract: Human-wildlife conflicts (HWC) have often negative impacts on both wildlife conservation and human livelihoods, representing a highly relevant management challenge. The present commentary aims to assess the scientific coverage of HWC by the European Journal of Wildlife Research (EJWR) through a literature review of 93 studies published between 2005 and 2024. The results show an increasing trend in numbers of HWC publications during this period, reflecting a potential increasing interest in this topic from the early 21st century. In addition, this review reveals several coverage gaps on EJWR publications, with a general focus on conflict-related impacts instead of assessing human-human conflicts. Moreover, to date the journal has published a higher proportion of studies conducted in Europe (57.14%) and Asia (27.47%), with studies from Africa and America being underrepresented (15.38%). Furthermore, most articles have addressed mainly carnivores and ungulates, and associated damage to livestock and agriculture. These are often large and charismatic species attracting higher research interest and funding. This publication bias may potentially limit the development of comprehensive solutions for diverse conflict situations. Overall, these research gaps should be addressed for generating evidence-based knowledge that promotes effective mitigation and coexistence strategies between human activities and the conservation of wildlife species in different geographic contexts.

items.title: Climate Protest and Firm ESG Performance: Elucidating Global North–South Inequalities
items.abstract: ABSTRACT In response to calls to keep global warming below 1.5°C, firms have employed responsible business practices in their operations. Neglecting their normative and ontological ethical obligations to their stakeholders has often attracted climate protests, posing a potential risk to business operations and their reputation by threatening their social licence. This study examines how climate protests influence corporate environmental management performance, highlighting disparities among firms in the Global North (GN) and Global South (GS). We use panel regression with fixed effects to analyse data on 3485 large firms worldwide between 2020 and 2024, comprising climate protest data from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) performance data obtained from the London Stock Exchange Group. Our study finds that climate protests are positively and significantly associated with firms' environmental performance. Protest size also correlates positively, though to a lesser extent. Notably, protests in the GN exert a stronger influence and impact than those in the GS. Additionally, a firm's human rights record positively predicts its environmental performance, highlighting the interconnectedness of corporate social and environmental responsibility. The results further reveal significant variation across firms, with the association between climate protests and environmental performance being most pronounced among firms with lower ESG ratings. Our findings underscore the need for firms and investors to integrate the potential of climate activism into their environmental risk management strategies and highlight regional disparities in corporate climate responsiveness.

items.title: Harnessing biotic interactions for kauri restoration under dieback pressure: a companion planting field trial in Waipoua Forest, Aotearoa New Zealand
items.abstract: Global native forest decline threatens ecosystems worldwide, including Aotearoa New Zealand’s kauri (Agathis australis) forests, which are under pressure of dieback disease caused by Phytophthora agathidicida (PA). Forest restoration has become a global priority, with degraded landscapes urgently needing rehabilitation to restore ecosystem functions, biodiversity, and resilience. Climate change is driving more extremes on environmental conditions, exposing juvenile trees under increasing stress. This is challenging to forest restoration efforts, but companion planting can be used as a strategy to enhance forest restoration outcomes. This method has been evidenced to promote facilitative interactions among neighbouring plants for improved aboveground establishment, while also enhancing belowground soil microbial communities through recruitment of beneficial microbial communities. I want to inspect if these reported benefits can be applied to early-stage juvenile establishments. Here, this thesis investigated whether co-planting kauri seedlings with selected native species and manipulating their relative arrival times could improve early kauri restoration outcomes in Waipoua Forest, New Zealand. Karamū (Coprosma robusta) and māpou (Myrsine australis) were chosen as companion plants due to their potential PA-inhibiting properties. A replicated field trial was established using three companion planting systems (karamū-only, māpou-only and mixed karamū-māpou systems) and kauri monoculture control. Kauri survival and growth were monitored across four sites (both detected and undetected with PA) for two years. For manipulation of arrival time, kauri was planted either concurrently with companion plants or one year later into pre-established companion vegetation, and their responses were inspected a year later. As for belowground responses, kauri-associated soil bacterial and fungal communities were characterised using high-throughput 16S rRNA and ITS amplicon sequencing, with the aims of assessing changes in microbial diversity, composition and abundances at one non-PA detected site. Through both aboveground and belowground responses, I examined the net outcome of facilitation and competition between kauri and native neighbours. VII Site-specific conditions were the strongest determinant of early kauri performance at two years. Kauri survival and growth differed significantly among sites but not companion planting treatments, indicating that environmental filtering and local biotic stress still overrode the short-term treatment effects. Overall, companion plant identity alone had weak and context-dependent effects on both aboveground (kauri survival and growth) and belowground (kauri soil microbial communities) in the concurrent-arrival cohort. Single-species companion plant systems showed weak signs of growth benefit for kauri in some sites, whereas the combined karamū-māpou treatment tended to perform less favourably for kauri survival across all sites, suggesting weak competitive effects during early establishment. In contrast, manipulating arrival time revealed potential facilitative priority effects. Late-arriving kauri often showed higher growth than concurrently planted kauri across all companion planting systems. Belowground, in single-species companion planting systems, late kauri arrival was associated with higher bacterial and fungal richness and modest shifts in microbial community composition, whereas no comparable effects were detected in mixed-species companion planting systems. Importantly, I also observed differential enrichment of plant-beneficial microbial taxa including Pseudomonas, Flavobacterium, and Glomeromycota with the strongest responses observed in the māpou system. Overall, this thesis shows that early kauri restoration was shaped less by companion plant identity alone than by the interaction between site conditions and companion species identity and diversity, alongside plant arrival time. More broadly, it contributes to knowledge in kauri restoration and community ecology by showing that understanding plant-plant and plant-microbe interactions can help inform early forest restoration outcomes.

items.title: Land use transitions drive ecosystem service supply–demand balance: spatiotemporal assessment and risk zoning in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area (Hubei section)
items.abstract: Growing human interference with natural ecosystems has positioned land use transition as a dominant force shaping the supply–demand equilibrium of ecosystem services (ESs). Focusing on the ecologically vulnerable Three Gorges Reservoir Area (Hubei section), this study examined how land use changes from 2000 to 2020 influenced water yield (WY), carbon storage (CS), food production (FP), and soil retention (SR). By integrating land use datasets, the InVEST model, the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation formula, and multiple regression approaches, we found that (1) land use dynamics were mainly driven by mutual transitions between cropland and forest, along with the expansion of impervious surfaces; (2) ES supply–demand ratios (ESDR) displayed pronounced spatiotemporal variations, with SR remaining in deficit while CS, FP, and WY improved; (3) redundancy analysis verified land use as the leading driver, accounting for over 55% of variance; (4) critical land conversion pathways exerted distinct directional influences on ESDR; and (5) spatial clustering analysis revealed that ESDR changes exhibited strong spatial autocorrelation. High–high clusters of CS and FP changes were primarily concentrated around residential cores, covering 10.68% and 8.22% of the study area, respectively; high–high clusters of WY changes dominated the eastern section, covering 23.72% of the area; and low–low clusters of SR changes dominated the southeastern section, covering 15.85% of the area. Based on spatial clustering of ESDR changes, the region was classified into ecological stability, high-risk, composite risk, and single-risk zones to support customized land management for national spatial optimization.

items.title: dataset from: Biodiversity research in the Cordillera del Cóndor and Cordillera de Kutukú (Ecuador–Peru), 1974–2025: a scoping-review database of 132 publications
items.abstract: This dataset contains the 132 publications (1974–2025) on the biodiversity of the Cordillera del Cóndor and the Cordillera de Kutukú, two sub-Andean mountain ranges in southeastern Ecuador and northern Peru, compiled for a scoping review following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Publications were identified through Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, Google Scholar (first 200 records per search), Ecuadorian institutional repositories and government/NGO sources (searches January–April 2026; publications up to 31 December 2025), complemented by backward citation searching, expert consultation and a supplementary targeted search (October 2026). A random 20% subsample was independently double-classified (Cohen's kappa = 0.82). Each record includes: code, citation, authors, year, title and source, link (DOI or URL), document type, country, cordillera, thematic category (taxonomy and systematics; biodiversity; biogeography and distribution; natural history; ecology; education and outreach), taxonomic group, whether new taxa were described, institutional collaboration (range-country, foreign or mixed), number of authors, identification route, and nationality of range-country institutions (Ecuador, Peru or both). The dataset supports the article "Species Discovery Outpaces Ecological Knowledge: A Scoping Review of Five Decades of Biodiversity Research in the Cordillera del Cóndor and Cordillera de Kutukú (Ecuador–Peru)", submitted to Diversity (MDPI). A README file describes all variables and categories.

items.title: The microbiome of draught no- and low-alcohol beer
items.abstract: The microbiological ecosystem of commercially available draught dispensed no- and low-alcohol beers was evaluated, with a focus on identifying predominant microorganisms with spoilage potential and characterizing variation in community structure. More than 50 samples, representing 20 no- and low- alcohol beers (7 different beer styles: lager, India pale ale, pale ale, wheat, radler, pilsner and amber ale; and 17 brands) were collected for analysis across 12 different public houses (accounts) in Nottingham, UK. Bacterial and fungal identification was achieved via third generation sequencing technologies, using amplicon-based nanopore sequencing (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). Analysis of samples indicated that species of Acetobacter, Brettanomyces and Saccharomyces were core microbiome members. The account from which a beer was sampled was shown to harbor distinct microbial communities and was the dominant factor in determining microbial community structure, explaining 72.6% of variation. This is the first study to apply third-generation sequencing technology for the analysis of draught no- and low-alcohol beers. The findings underscore the vulnerability of draught products to microbial spoilage, and highlight the importance of implementing strict hygiene control focused on draught lines, taps, keg couplers and nozzles, especially when dispensing microbiologically sensitive no- and low-alcohol beverages.

items.title: Spatio-temporal Analysis of Land Use and Land Cover Change in the Achanakmaar-Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve, Central India: Implications for Forest Degradation and Conservation Planning
items.abstract: Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) Change plays a crucial role in influencing ecological stability, biodiversity, and climate dynamics. This study investigates the spatio-temporal dynamics of LULC in the Achanakmaar-Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve (AABR), a critical ecological zone in Central India using 2001 and 2021 Landsat imagery, geospatial tools- ArcGIS, and maximum likelihood classification approach. Effort was made to map and analyze changes in major land cover types, viz., dense mixed forest (DMF), sal mixed forest (SMF), bamboo brakes (BB), teak plantation (TP), open mixed forest (OMF), agricultural land (AG), human habitations (HH), and water bodies (WB). The results revealed a significant decline in forested area, particularly DMF (-43.93 km²), SMF (-50.77 km²), BB (-6.07 km²), TP (-40.63 km²), and WB (-3.20 km²), while OMF (+131.14 km²), AG (+23.65 km²), and habitations (+2.88 km²) showed notable expansion in two decades. These trends are consistent with anthropogenic pressures reported in similar tropical forest ecosystems. The findings of this study corroborate with the global studies that tropical forests are under increasing threat due to unsustainable land use transitions. Our findings underscore the urgent need for policy interventions and ecological restoration through community-based forest management, reforestation, and promotion of sustainable agroforestry practices. This study contributes novel insights into the regional forest degradation patterns in Central India and demonstrates the utility of remote sensing for long-term environmental monitoring.

items.title: Season-dependent trait–environment filtering influences interaction networks in mixed-species bird flocks
items.abstract: Seasonal variation can strongly influence species interactions, yet its effects on interaction networks remain poorly understood in tropical and subtropical systems. We surveyed mixed-species bird flocks (MSFs) across 20 2 × 2 km grid cells in a subtropical forest in southern China during breeding and non-breeding seasons, quantified seasonal changes in flock composition and network structure, and examined how species traits and environmental factors drive these changes. More species and individuals joined mixed-species bird flocks in the non-breeding season, producing more connected and cohesive networks. During the breeding season, network structure was associated with breeding traits: species with larger clutch sizes showed higher association strength, but overall network connectivity and cohesion declined, suggesting trade-offs imposed by parental care. Network structure in the non-breeding season was related to morphological traits, with smaller species forming more cohesive networks. Environmental effects were also season dependent. Connectivity increased with elevation, forest cover and canopy cover in the breeding season, whereas in the non-breeding season networks were most connected and cohesive at low elevations with high tree species richness and vegetation productivity. Our results demonstrate the importance of seasonal effects on mixed-species bird flocks and highlight the need to maintain mountain connectivity, as communities may rely on different parts of mountains across seasons.

items.title: ESTABLISHMENT AND ORGANIZATION OF THE NATIONAL DIATOM HERBARIUM OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA (DHBH)
items.abstract: Description The Diatom Herbarium of Bosnia and Herzegovina (DHBH) is a specialized scientific collection established to preserve, organize, and document permanent diatom slides originating from historical research, undergraduate and postgraduate theses, doctoral dissertations, scientific projects, publications, and educational activities. Housed in the Laboratory for the Systematics and Ecology of Algae, Fungi and Lichens, Department of Biology, Faculty of Science, University of Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the collection comprises 3,520 permanent slides representing freshwater and marine environments, with sampling records spanning 1962–2023. The collection is organized into eight series (A–H), reflecting the diverse origins and research contexts of the preserved material. An accompanying electronic database documents accession numbers, sampling localities, geographical information, habitat types, sampling dates, collectors, and associated slide numbers, providing a structured digital reference for the physical collection. This dataset accompanies the scientific article “Establishment and Organization of the National Diatom Herbarium of Bosnia and Herzegovina (DHBH)” and supports collection management, traceability, data accessibility, and the future reuse of historical and contemporary diatom records. By combining preserved microscopic material with standardized digital documentation, DHBH provides a valuable foundation for taxonomic, ecological, biogeographical, and biodiversity research, as well as education and the continued study of diatoms in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

items.title: Assessing Diversity, Carbon Stock Quantification and Economic Valuation of Mangrove Forest along the Coastal Areas of Davao Oriental, Philippines
items.abstract: This study assessed the diversity, aboveground carbon stock, and economic value of mangrove forests along the coastal areas of Davao Oriental, Philippines. Field-based mangrove inventories were conducted using three 100-m transects comprising 20 plots and a total sampled area of 2000 m². The sampling was intended to characterize the mangrove community at the assessed field sites and is not treated as statistically representative of all mangrove forests in the province. Remote sensing using the Mangrove Vegetation Index (MVI) and Landsat 8 imagery was used to delineate mangrove extent. The mangrove community comprised seven species and had a Shannon–Wiener diversity index (H′) of 1.65 and Pielou’s evenness index (J′) of 0.85, indicating moderate diversity and relatively high evenness. Sonneratia alba was the most abundant and structurally dominant species and contributed 12,908.43 kg (88.86%) of the estimated 14,524.63 kg aboveground carbon stock in the sampled plots. The current GIS output indicates a total mapped mangrove extent of 3065.82 ha; however, municipal-level values require verification against the original GIS zonal-statistics output before publication. The field-based carbon estimate was not extrapolated to the remotely sensed provincial extent. Using an assumed conservative carbon-market scenario of US$5 tCO2e⁻¹ and a social-cost scenario of US$51 tCO2e⁻¹, the sampled carbon stock was valued at US$266.45 and US$2717.79, respectively. The findings highlight the ecological and socioeconomic importance of mangroves for biodiversity conservation, carbon storage, fisheries, coastal protection, and local livelihood support.

items.title: Spatiotemporal patterns of aboveground vegetation and soil seed banks in desert steppe under photovoltaic disturbance
items.abstract: The unique microenvironment created by photovoltaic (PV) power stations may progressively reshape ecosystem species composition through sustained effects on aboveground vegetation and soil seed banks. However, the long-term ecological impacts, particularly those on soil seed banks, remain poorly understood. We investigated aboveground vegetation and soil seed banks across three PV power stations with different operational durations (5, 10, and 15 years) in desert steppe ecosystems to assess how PV-induced microhabitats filter vegetation and seed bank assemblages. Our results show that with increasing operational duration, the density of soil seed bank outside the PV stations remained stable, whereas it increased progressively between panels, from 1657 seeds·m - ² at 5 years to 2279 seeds·m - ² at 10 years and 2880 seeds·m - ² at 15 years, and declined significantly beneath panels. Across all operational durations, seed bank density consistently followed the spatial gradient: between panels > outside the PV stations > beneath panels. The spatial distribution of aboveground vegetation mirrored that of the seed bank and patterns of α-diversity exhibited similar trends. Significant differences in community species composition were observed among locations within each operational duration, and community differentiation intensified over time. Early-stage divergence was primarily driven by a few dominant species but gradually shifted toward regulation by multiple species. In addition, the functional composition of both the aboveground community and soil seed banks changed: the proportion of perennial prostrate taproot clonal plants increased beneath panels with operational duration, whereas annual prostrate taproot non-clonal plants increased significantly between panels. Overall, PV stations progressively restructure plant communities and soil seed banks by creating spatially heterogeneous microenvironments, with ecological effects intensifying over time. These findings provide valuable insights for the ecological management and sustainable land-use planning of PV installations in arid and semi-arid regions.

items.title: Beyond Model Accuracy: Comparing GTAP and GLOBIOM for Environmental Governance, Transparency, and Climate Justice in the Global South-A Critical Review
items.abstract: Global land-use models increasingly shape assessments of biofuel sustainability, agricultural trade, deforestation and climate mitigation, yet the implications of their methodological choices for the Global South remain insufficiently examined. This qualitative literature review critically compares the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) family, especially GTAP-BIO, with the Global Biosphere Management Model (GLOBIOM). Drawing on peer-reviewed research published from 2020 to 2026, the analysis integrates economic-model architecture, indirect land-use change, ecological accounting, uncertainty, reproducibility and environmental justice. Seven thematic findings emerge: structural non-equivalence; sensitivity of land-use and carbon estimates to assumptions; incompleteness of carbon-centric environmental indicators; spatial and social asymmetries in policy impacts; uneven representation of smallholders and Indigenous peoples; insufficiently standardised transparency; and opportunities for complementary rather than competitive model use. Evidence from Indonesia, Brazil and Africa suggests that model-based trade and climate rules can interact with pre-existing inequalities, although such effects are contingent rather than inherent to either model. The paper proposes a Transparent and Just Environmental Modelling Framework requiring scenario harmonisation, ecological triangulation, uncertainty disclosure, participatory appraisal, distributive safeguards and independent review. It concludes that modelling legitimacy depends on fitness for purpose, traceable evidence and accountable policy interpretation, not solely on numerical precision or model complexity.

items.title: Ticks of Kazakhstan: a systematic review, evidence-based taxonomic checklist, and assessment of molecular confirmation gaps
items.abstract: Background Published estimates of Kazakhstan’s tick diversity vary because historical names, synonyms, regional records, unverified range statements, and unevenly sampled modern datasets have often been combined without consistent evidence criteria. We aimed to produce an auditable national checklist that separates verified occurrence from provisional, unresolved, and non-independent records. Methods We systematically reviewed English-, Russian-, and Kazakh-language sources reporting ticks from the present-day territory of Kazakhstan, with no lower publication-date limit and with searches conducted through 28 July 2026. Historical monographs, field surveys, molecular studies, collection-based records, and taxonomic works were evaluated at the taxon–locality–evidence level. Original names were retained and reconciled with current taxonomy. Records were graded according to locality and specimen traceability, identification method, molecular evidence for the tick itself, and availability of sequence or voucher information. Results The evidence database contained 62 source records and 206 taxon–locality evidence records. After reconciliation of 59 source-name entries, 42 species in ten genera and two families were retained: 23 met the strict criteria for verified occurrence and 19 were provisionally verified. Ten additional currently valid taxa were presented separately because their Kazakhstan occurrence requires primary-source confirmation, specimen re-examination, or taxonomic reassessment. Recently strengthened records included Hyalomma dromedarii, Dermacentor nuttalli, D. niveus, Ixodes occultus, I. crenulatus, Haemaphysalis concinna, Rhipicephalus annulatus, and Argas reflexus . Molecular identification of the tick was available for 13 of 23 verified species (56.5%) and 14 of all 42 retained species (33.3%). Evidence remained geographically and host-biased despite improved coverage of western and northern Kazakhstan. Conclusion Kazakhstan’s tick fauna cannot be represented reliably by a single inherited species total. The updated evidence-graded checklist provides a reproducible baseline for taxonomy, biodiversity assessment, veterinary and public-health surveillance, and targeted voucher-based molecular resampling in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

items.title: The bottom-up effects of aridity and the top-down effects of grazing shape biodiversity across trophic levels in the Inner Mongolian grassland
items.abstract: Aridity poses a severe threat to global biodiversity, and grazing further exacerbates ecological stress in drylands. Plants and soil organisms regulate nutrient cycling and ecosystem stability through trophic cascade effects. It remains unclear whether aridity and grazing have consistent effects across trophic levels. We selected 65 paired grazing and ungrazing sites along a natural aridity gradient in the Inner Mongolian grassland in which we explored the diversity of plants, soil bacteria, fungi, nematodes and the impacts of aridity and grazing on trophic cascade effects. Increasing aridity significantly decreased the species richness of plants, pathotrophic fungi, saprotrophic fungi, herbivorous and bacterivorous nematodes. Grazing significantly increased bacterial richness and reduced the richness of herbivorous and omnivorous-predatory nematodes. Overall, aridity exerted a stronger impact on biodiversity compared with grazing. Aridity induced bottom-up effects by initially reducing plant richness, with cascading effects on soil fungal richness and higher trophic communities. Grazing reduced omnivorous-predatory nematode richness, which decreased the richness of lower trophic level organisms through top-down effects. Our research highlights different multi-trophic cascades of aridity and grazing in grasslands, emphasizing the necessity for deeper investigation into biodiversity responses across trophic levels under global change and land use.

items.title: Measurement induced faster symmetry restoration in quantum trajectories
items.abstract: Continuous measurement of quantum systems provides a standard route to quantum trajectories through the successive acquisition of information which further results in measurement back-action. In this work, we harness this back-action as a resource for global $U(1)$ symmetry restoration where continuous measurement is combined with a $U(1)$-preserving unitary evolution. Starting from a $U(1)$ symmetry-broken initial state, we simulate quantum trajectories generated by continuous measurements of both global and local observables. We show that under global monitoring, states containing superpositions of distant charge sectors restore symmetry faster than those involving nearby sectors. We establish the universality of this behavior across different measurement protocols. Finally, we demonstrate that local monitoring can further accelerate symmetry restoration for certain states that relax slowly under global monitoring.

items.title: Unveiling Hidden Lyman Alpha Emitters in the DESI DR1 Data
items.abstract: Abstract We present an automatic method based on machine learning convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to detect Ly α emitters (LAEs) hidden in the Data Release 1 spectroscopic data set of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). Those LAEs mostly have incorrect redshift estimations because the current DESI pipeline is not designed to detect and measure the redshifts of galaxies at z > 2. To uncover those sources, we first visually inspect 4134 DESI spectra and construct a sample, consisting of both LAEs and non-LAEs, for training and testing the CNN-based model to (1) detect LAEs in DESI spectra and (2) determine their Ly α redshifts. The final model yields 95.2% purity and 95.9% completeness for detecting LAEs. We apply this model to approximately 2 × 10 6 spectra of sources targeted as emission-line galaxies and detect 19,685 LAEs from z ∼ 2 to 3.5 within 12 minutes with a single GPU, illustrating the high efficiency of this model for identifying LAEs. The detected LAEs are mostly at the bright end of the luminosity function with Ly α luminosity L Ly α ≳ 10 43 erg s −1 . The high signal-to-noise composite spectrum of the detected LAEs further shows various spectral features, including P-Cygni profiles of metal lines and Mg ii emission lines, possible indicators of Lyman continuum escape fraction, revealing the rich astrophysical information in this LAE sample. Finally, this sample can be used to train and validate the pipelines for redshift determination of LAEs for the preparation of the DESI-II survey.

items.title: Spectral energy-loss bump and γ-ray pulsar halos
items.abstract: Abstract The parent electron spectrum of $\gamma$-ray pulsar halos is determined by continuous injection and radiative energy losses, with the nonlinear nature of the latter expected to produce an age-dependent energy-loss bump in the halo spectrum. We demonstrate that the broadband $\gamma$-ray spectrum of the Geminga halo measured by Fermi-LAT and HAWC is consistent with this expectation. Its energy-loss bump appears in the GeV region and is primarily produced by electrons injected at the earliest stage. Therefore, fitting the data allows us to constrain parameters governing early electron injection, such as the pulsar braking index $n$ and initial spin period $P_0$. In addition, we show that another crucial condition for explaining the Geminga halo spectrum is a power-law index of the injection spectrum close to $1$, consistent with the X-ray observations of the Geminga pulsar wind nebula. Currently, no significant energy-loss bump has been detected in the spectrum of the Monogem halo; based on this, we also place preliminary constraints on $n$ and $P_0$ for Monogem. This work demonstrates that pulsar halo spectra can be used not only to constrain electron injection parameters but also to provide independent estimates of certain intrinsic pulsar properties.

items.title: An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A
items.abstract: Abstract We present a multiwavelength study of GRB 260310A, a nearby long-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) at z ≃ 0.153 associated with a broad-lined Type Ic supernova. Despite its modest prompt gamma-ray output, E γ ,iso ≃ 3.5 × 10 50 erg, GRB 260310A exhibits one of the brightest afterglows ever observed in the X-ray, optical, and radio bands. Its apparent brightness is not its only remarkable feature. The optical afterglow displays a delayed onset, characterized by a slow rising phase, with slope α ≈ −1, and a late peak at ∼0.1 day. We argue that the combination of weak prompt emission, hard peak energy, and late afterglow onset is naturally explained by a GRB jet viewed off-axis. The radio spectral energy distributions are consistent with synchrotron radiation and indicate the presence of both reverse- shock (RS) and forward-shock (FS) components, thus providing a first test of RS models in an off-axis geometry. The X-ray afterglow displays a prominent rebrightening, monitored for up to ∼68 days with no evidence of spectral evolution. A low level of linear polarization, Π ≈ 1.7%, is measured at 15 GHz at T 0 + 55 days and suggests that, at these late times, the FS is the dominant emission component from radio to X-rays. This late-time rebrightening represents a critical test for the two-component jet model. If interpreted as the emergence of a narrow jet core viewed further off-axis, it would imply extreme luminosities and energetics for an on-axis observer.

items.title: How Common Are Common Envelopes? Quantifying Their Role in Forming Gravitational-Wave Sources
items.abstract: A central goal of gravitational-wave astronomy is to use merging binary black hole (BBH), black hole-neutron star (BHNS), and binary neutron star (BNS) systems as fossils to reconstruct the formation and evolution of massive stars across cosmic time. In practice, this inference relies on population-synthesis models that map massive stellar binaries to merging compact objects. However, these models disagree on the dominant orbital-hardening mechanisms within isolated binary evolution, particularly on whether common-envelope (CE) evolution is required. To address this, we compile and systematically compare formation-channel predictions from more than 200 isolated-binary population-synthesis simulations, organized within a unified hierarchical taxonomy. We find that BBH and BHNS formation pathways span nearly the full allowed range from CE-dominated to without-CE-dominated evolution (0-100%), while often predicting similar merger rates, revealing a fundamental degeneracy: merger-rate measurements alone do not uniquely constrain the underlying evolutionary pathways. In contrast, BNS formation proceeds almost exclusively through channels involving at least one CE phase (>90-100%), suggesting CE evolution plays a qualitatively different role in BNS than in BBH and BHNS formation. The relative contributions of with-CE and without-CE pathways are governed primarily by assumptions controlling mass-transfer stability, angular-momentum loss, CE efficiency, and supernova physics, which often act non-linearly and in correlated fashion, such that trends from one-at-a-time parameter variations do not generalize across simulation frameworks. Robust interpretation of gravitational-wave populations will therefore require transparent formation-channel definitions, reproducible analysis pipelines, systematic cross-code comparisons, and observational constraints that extend beyond merger rates alone.

items.title: In-flight calibration of the Wide-field X-ray Telescope on board the Einstein Probe
items.abstract: By utilizing novel lobster-eye optics, the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) on board the Probe satellite achieves an unprecedented combination of a large instantaneous field of view (FoV) and high sensitivity for monitoring the dynamic X-ray sky. In this paper, we present the in-orbit calibration results of the WXT during its first two and a half years of operations. By conducting observations of standard celestial sources---i.e., the Crab Nebula, Scorpius X-1, and Cassiopeia A---we systematically characterized key instrumental properties. Our analysis demonstrates that the in-orbit performance of the WXT agrees with prelaunch ground calibrations. The spatial resolution, denoted by the full width at half maximum of the focal spot, typically ranges from 3' to 6' across ∼90% of the FoV, with a median of ∼ 4.3'. The post-calibration source positioning accuracy achieves 1.3' (at the 90% confidence level). The in-orbit effective area is consistent with model predictions and ground measurements, exhibiting an overall systematic uncertainty of łesssim 10% (90% C.L.) in the 0.5--4,keV band. While the vast majority of the detectors remain highly stable, a noticeable long-term degradation at the low-energy end (sim30%--40%, 0.4--0.6,keV) is observed in a few specific modules. Furthermore, spectral evaluations using Cas A confirm the stability of the energy scale and spectral resolution of the focal-plane complementary metal-oxide semiconductor detectors. All derived calibration products have been incorporated into the WXT calibration database (CALDB). These results comprehensively verify the instrumental capabilities of the WXT, providing a solid foundation for the reliable analysis of scientific observations. Einstein

items.title: Self-force on a static scalar charge in traversable wormholes
items.abstract: The self-force acting on a charged particle is sensitive to the global structure of curved spacetime and can serve as a probe of geometry beyond local curvature. We compute the static scalar self-force on a point charge in the two-parameter family of spherically symmetric wormholes introduced by Konoplya and Zhidenko, members of the broader Morris-Thorne class of traversable wormholes. Using mode-sum regularization, we analyze its dependence on the shape exponent $q$, which controls the throat geometry, and the redshift parameter $p$, which determines the redshift function and tidal strength. We find that the self-force is generally not unidirectional: it can change sign with radial distance from the throat, with up to two distinct zero crossings depending on $(p,q)$. We provide a systematic characterization of how both the direction and large-distance falloff depend on the wormhole parameters. For sufficiently large $p$, the force can decay at a slower rate than the canonical $\sim r^{-3}$ behavior typical of isolated-body spacetimes, with stronger flaring (more negative $q$) leading to more rapid decay. In the combined limit $p \to \infty$ and $q \to -\infty$, the asymptotic falloff approaches that of the static scalar self-force in the Ellis wormhole.

items.title: Emulation of non-linear 1D spectral models: relativistic X-ray reflection
items.abstract: Abstract The use of machine learning techniques to approximate computationally expensive models has become increasingly prevalent in a wide variety of fields within astronomy. We discuss the implementation of emulators for 1-dimensional models in the context of the astrophysical numerical model reltrans, a black hole X-ray spectral model that models the effects of relativistically smeared emission from an accretion disk. We argue that the decision of whether and how to emulate should follow from a systematic characterisation of the target model, and we demonstrate a diagnostic workflow: examining how the spectrum varies with individual parameters. We adopt a modular strategy, emulating only the relativistically convolved reflection spectrum (≈1 − 10% of the total flux) rather than the full model. Using an operator-learning architecture with Fourier feature embeddings and FiLM conditioning, we reproduce the reflection spectrum to O(0.1)% precision across 0.1-100 keV with a 4-10x speed-up that scales considerably better under vectorised evaluation. This emulator, RTFAST2, recovers the true parameters of simulated observations without the systematic posterior biases of our previous work. We conclude that no architecture is universally transferable and bespoke emulators motivated by a model’s specific structure are required. The modular approach taken in this work presents a promising strategy for future emulators of numerical models.

items.title: Simulating the LOcal Web (SLOW). VII. Intergalactic magnetic field models for multi-messenger applications
items.abstract: The propagation of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays and ultrahigh-energy γ-rays remains an open question in astroparticle physics, with the intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) playing a crucial role in deflecting charged particles and shaping electromagnetic cascade spectra. Characterizing the IGMF across cosmic large-scale structure is therefore essential for interpreting multi-messenger observations and constraining the magnetogenesis scenarios that seeded it. We aim to provide accurate IGMF models to the astroparticle physics community and to test their properties and robustness. We analyzed IGMF models derived from the constrained cosmological simulation Simulating the LOcal Web (SLOW) alongside a set of rescaled magnetic-field models. We further introduce a novel algorithm to determine an for galaxies lying below the constraining power of the initial conditions, which enables accurate line-of-sight magnetic-field extraction toward relevant sources. ideal position The models span a wide range of filling factors and sample distinct regions of the electron density–magnetic field strength phase space in filaments, while converging in the cores of galaxy clusters; the simulated field from SLOW best reproduces the IGMF derived from the electromagnetic γ-ray cascade. Models extracted using the introduced ideal position yield improved accuracy and may benefit multi-messenger studies more broadly. The large-scale structure drift of the simulated clusters exploited by the algorithm also offers a potential route to refine the simulation's constrained initial conditions.

items.title: Bayesian inference of the dense matter equation of state built upon extended Skyrme interactions: A generalization
items.abstract: The nonrelativistic theory of nuclear matter (NM) based on Brussels-Skyrme interactions is employed to develop models for dense and neutron-rich matter within a Bayesian framework. We employ the following set of constraints: the four best-known nuclear empirical parameters, density dependence of the energy per particle in pure neutron matter (PNM), density dependence of the Landau effective mass ($m_\mathrm{eff}$) of neutrons in PNM and symmetric NM, and a lower limit on the maximum gravitational mass that neutron stars (NSs) can sustain. In addition, a number of ``sanity checks'' are added: the values of the speed of sound, neutron and proton Landau effective masses and Fermi velocities are constrained up to the central density of the most massive NS configuration and for isospin asymmetries $δ=(n_n-n_p)/(n_n+n_p)$ ranging from 0 to 1. Our ensemble of models \emph{fully} explores the capacity of non-relativistic Brussels-Skyrme effective interactions to describe NM at densities exceeding several times the nuclear saturation density. This is a necessary step toward a better understanding of the properties of dense matter and possible correlations between the parameters of NSs and the parameters of NM. Due to pronounced U-shaped density-dependencies of $m_\mathrm{eff}$, all our models exhibit a non-monotonic ``rise-and-fall'' behavior of the thermal pressure ($p_\mathrm{th}$) as a function of density, which in extreme cases leads to $p_\mathrm{th} < 0$. This work is a generalization of [Beznogov and Raduta, Phys. Rev. C 110, 035805 (2024)].

items.title: 1000 cataclysmic variables identified from DESI spectroscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Most cataclysmic variables (CVs) are discovered when they have an outburst generating an inherent selection bias against CVs that rarely, or never, outburst. CVs discovered by virtue of their spectroscopic characteristics are particularly valuable to offset this bias and we have used an established machine-learning technique to assist in searching 98 966 000 spectra obtained by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Survey (DESI) to find such CVs. DESI observations are much deeper than previous spectroscopic surveys and we have identified 1028 CVs, 221 of which are new including ten of the AMCVn subtype. We have spectroscopically confirmed 440 CV candidates and obtained 85 new or improved orbital periods.We present revised space density estimates based upon this new data. We have also added ten more to the eight known examples of an intriguing class of CVs which exhibit peculiar changes in accretion.

items.title: Rare processes in ultrahigh-energy tau-lepton transport
items.abstract: Abstract In cosmic neutrino observatories, charged-lepton transport is a key input for interpreting observables and reconstructing neutrino events. Charged leptons propagating through matter undergo several energy loss processes, such as electron pair production and photonuclear interaction. In this work, we investigate several rare processes in tau-lepton transport, focusing primarily on muon pair production, $\tau N \to \tau \mu^+\mu^- N$, and Primakoff neutral-pion production, $\tau N \to \tau \pi^0 N$. At EeV energies, we find that the energy loss contributions from muon pair and Primakoff pion production are only $0.6\%$ and $0.2\%$, respectively, of that from electron pair production. Nevertheless, dimuon production may be relevant to tau neutrino searches in underwater and under-ice Cherenkov telescopes. The interaction length for dimuon emission by an EeV tau is only $6~{\rm km}$ in standard rock. Such events may be identified through the lateral separation of dimuon tracks or through a kebab topology if tau decays in the detector. In addition, we also emphasize that hard photonuclear scatterings during tau transport become increasingly important at the energy scales relevant for lunar neutrino searches like SKA-Low. items.title: Orbital Migration of Interacting Stellar Mass Black Holes in Disks around Supermassive Black Holes. III. Mass Distribution of Hierarchical Mergers
items.abstract: Abstract Active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks are a promising location for the formation of binary black holes (BBHs) that will merge on relatively short timescales and be detected by LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA (LVK). To compare the mass function (MF) of black holes (BHs) undergoing hierarchical mergers in AGN disks to the inferred MFs from LVK observations, we perform 360 simulations with an N -body code augmented to include an analytic model for migration torques and other gas forces. We focus on the region surrounding migration traps in AGN disks where migration torques cancel out and BHs converge. We find that regardless of changes in the initial MF and BBH merger criteria, frequent mergers deplete the number of BHs with masses ≲10 M ⊙ and fill the upper mass gap with a roughly uniform distribution from 40–100 M ⊙ , with a slight overabundance around ≈70 M ⊙ from resonant orbiters. We also find an average merger rate of ∼6 Gpc −3 yr −1 for migration-trap-aided BBH mergers in our AGN disk model. ∼40%of these mergers have uneven mass ratios and 16% have a primary mass ∈[50−100] M ⊙ . Therefore, AGN disks could easily be the source of BBH mergers observed by LVK that are difficult to produce through traditional stellar evolution channels. Our simulations also form a separate higher-mass intermediate mass black hole (IMBH) population >200 M ⊙ after ∼2 Myr. Future gravitational wave detectors can use observations of this IMBH population to constrain models of AGN accretion disks.

items.title: Estimation of systematic error from bulk deformation of end test mass induced by photon calibrator for LIGO post-O5 gravitational wave projects
items.abstract: Abstract We studied bulk deformation of the end test masses (ETMs) of gravitational wave (GW) detectors caused by calibration devices named Photon Calibrator (Pcal). This bulk deformation is one of the source of calibration error since it induces non-linear displacement from the ideal pendulum motion of the ETM. Particularly, it is the dominant error source above 1500 Hz which is crucial to the studies of neutron star mergers. The displacement also depends on beam offsets of the main interferometer (IFO) beam and Pcal beams. We conceptually described frequency dependent effect of bulk deformation and evaluated it in several cases of the beam offset with finite-element analysis (FEA) software, for ETM models of Advanced LIGO (aLIGO), KAGRA, Advanced Virgo (AdVirgo), and LIGO A#.

items.title: Deep radio characterization of the supernova remnant G343.1-00.7
items.abstract: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are extended radio sources whose morphology and evolution are shaped by the interaction of strong shocks with the surrounding medium. Radio morphological and spectral studies are essential for investigating their local physical properties and particle acceleration mechanisms. We conducted a detailed radio morphological analysis of the SNR G343.1-00.7 and accurately determined its radio continuum spectral properties, both integrated and spatially resolved. We combined the 0.944 GHz Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathﬁnder (ASKAP) image from the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey with 0.088–0.200 GHz MWA-GLEAM data to characterize the integrated radio spectrum of G343.1-00.7 and perform its first sensitive spatially resolved spectral analysis. We derive an integrated spectral index of α=-0.50 for G343.1-00.7, confirming the previously reported value with significantly improved accuracy. We redefine the radio morphology of the remnant, providing the first morphological and spectral evidence that the filamentary structures overlapping the nearby G343.147-00.44 are physically associated with the SNR. Local brightness-brightness analysis further reveals flatter-spectrum filaments along the southeastern shell, consistent with a possible thermal bremsstrahlung contribution from radiative or partially radiative shocks. By comparison with and CO data, we identify atomic and molecular gas components kinematically consistent with the SNR distance, although no clear morphological evidence of interaction is found. The gas distribution around the however, suggests the presence of an expanding shell partially embedded within its parent molecular cloud. Overall, theoretical models based on our radio characterization place G343.1-00.7 between the late Sedov phase and the early pressure-driven phase of its evolution, suggesting that different regions may be at different evolutionary stages. Our results demonstrate the potential of high-resolution ASKAP observations for characterizing the morphology and spatially resolved spectral properties of SNRs, particularly for poorly studied remnants in complex Galactic environments.

items.title: Enhancing the Interpretability of Radial Velocity Analysis Using Leave-one-out Cross Validation
items.abstract: Abstract Radial velocity (RV) observations are reaching increasingly high precision, enabling the targeting of low-amplitude signals. Assessing results obtained at the limits of our capabilities requires understanding the relationship between data, models and inference. Leave-one-out cross validation (LOO-CV) has become an increasingly popular tool for interpretable model criticism in astronomical data analysis. In this work, we demonstrate how LOO-CV can provide insight into the RV analysis of exoplanetary systems through three case studies. We first investigate the anomalously high mass of HD 119130 b inferred from CARMENES RVs, later revised significantly downward after follow-up observations with other instruments. We show that this high mass was strongly driven by two individual measurements, whose removal significantly reduces the tension between data sets. Next, we use LOO-CV as a model selection tool for the GJ 4276 system. Here, LOO-CV prefers an eccentric single-planet model over a two-planet model, and identifies the orbital phases at which follow-up observations would best discriminate between them. Finally, we extend LOO-CV to models with correlated noise, applying it to the GJ 357 system, whose RVs are modeled with a Gaussian process. We find no predictive support for a fourth planetary signal that is moderately favored by the Bayesian evidence, strengthening the interpretation of a three-planet architecture previously reported in the literature. We provide practical guidance for implementing LOO-CV in RV analysis, together with an online tutorial. Such methods will become ever more important as future RV surveys push the limits of planet detection and characterization.

items.title: High-resolution Spectropolarimetric Observations of the Optical Filaments surrounding NGC 1275 with ESPaDOnS
items.abstract: Abstract We analyze archival high-spectral-resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetric observations ( R = λ /Δ λ = 68000) of three targeted locations within the filamentary nebula surrounding NGC 1275. We present here the analysis of the main filaments' emission lines, namely, [N ii ] λ 6584, H α , and [N ii ] λ 6548, across our three pointings displaying clear detectable emission, with one also showing an additional [S ii ] λ 6716 and [S ii ] λ 6731 emission line doublet. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm and thanks to the exceptionally high spectral resolution of the observations, we resolve for the first time each of the emission lines within one of the pointings into a set of three emission components with a remarkable velocity dispersion contrast ( σ 1 ∼ 25 km s −1 , σ 2 ∼ 90 km s −1 , and σ 3 ∼ 208 km s −1 ). We also perform flux ratios of the three detected emission components, which reveal differences in electron density and ionization sources. Consequently, the ESPaDOnS observations appear to reveal for the first time the overlap of an outer quiescent filament and a central turbulent filament likely affected by the active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity at a distance of ∼6 . ″ 8 (∼2.5 kpc) from the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). Finally, ESPaDOnS polarimetric data of one of the pointing allow us to confirm an average linear polarization degree of ∼0.15%–0.14% and an angle of polarization of 5 . ° 3 ± 25 . ° 7 for the optical emission of the filaments, as well as polarization dips associated with the H α emission line and its multiple emission components. We interpret these features and measurements as tentative polarization due to dust scattering.

items.title: Gamma-ray calorimetry of Seyfert winds
items.abstract: Two stacking analyses based on Large Area Telescope (LAT) data have detected GeV emission from local radio-quiet Seyferts. One was selected via an X-ray ultra-fast outflow (UFO) and one is hard-X-ray-bright. Similar luminosities are attributed to different mechanisms: wind-driven shocks and the accretion-disk corona. Fermi We investigated how efficiently Seyfert outflows convert mechanical power into GeV photons, whether the two detections require distinct mechanisms, and how Seyferts compare with low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs). We performed no new reduction of -LAT data but homogenized published measurements to 0.1--100 GeV, placed local mechanical accelerators on one L_γ-- Fermi diagram, and expressed η=L_γ/ as a fraction (̊ho) of the fiducial complete-calorimetry efficiency η_ inverting ̊ho for the ambient density required by pp losses. Winds from Seyfert active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have ̊ho=0.020^ +0.018 _ -0.011 for an acceleration efficiency of 0.1, a factor of simeq13.5 below starburst superwinds (̊ho=0.26^ +0.37 _ -0.16 ). The difference exceeds a factor of three with probability 0.95 and is independent of acceleration parameters common to both classes; it is conditional on the wind kinetic powers, collapsing only if every wind sits at its minimum launch radius. The implied densities, sim10 and sim10^2 cm -3 $, are consistency values, as density, shock radius, and speed are degenerate. The two stacking detections agree within a factor of 1.75 in γ-ray output per unit Eddington luminosity, but the 95 percent interval, 0.26--$24, is too wide to distinguish between them. A third stack, of 186 low-luminosity AGNs, extends the comparison 1.5 dex lower, ordered by AGN power. The GeV detectability of a non-jetted AGN is set by the product of mechanical power and calorimetric fraction. LINER outflows lack the power. For the adopted wind energetics, UFO-selected Seyfert winds fall short in calorimetry. Starburst superwinds succeed in both.

items.title: Multiline Spectropolarimetric Evidence for Photospheric Reconnection in Ellerman Bombs from DKIST
items.abstract: Abstract Ellerman bombs (EBs) are compact, transient brightenings observed in the wings of Balmer lines and are believed to result from magnetic reconnection in the lower solar atmosphere. However, their signatures have rarely been observed simultaneously in multiple spectral lines sensitive to the lower atmosphere. We present novel high-resolution multiline spectropolarimetric observations of EBs obtained with the Visible Spectro-Polarimeter (ViSP) on the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). Simultaneous observations reveal remarkable H β wing enhancements extending up to ∼4 Å from the line core and intensity enhancements in the Na i D1 and Fe i 6302 lines. Using multiline non-LTE inversion of the Na i and Fe i lines, we infer localized photospheric heating of up to Δ T ∼ 800 K, accompanied by weak upflows and downflows at EB locations. Comparing with synthetic observables from Bifrost radiative-MHD simulations, we find that synthetic spectra reproduce the observed H β and Na i D wing enhancements and yield atmospheric stratification broadly consistent with those inferred from the non-LTE inversion. This study provides strong evidence that EBs are driven by photospheric magnetic reconnection below the temperature-minimum region, and places new constraints on the realistic EB models and small-scale energy release in the lower solar atmosphere.

items.title: The MIni-Halos in MIni-Clusters (MIMIC) project. New insights into the origin of mini-halos from a LOFAR, uGMRT, and MeerKAT study of diffuse radio emission in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235
items.abstract: This work is aimed at investigating the presence of diffuse radio emission in low-mass (M_ 500 łeq3 M_⊙) relaxed galaxy clusters. 14 We present a pilot study for the MIMIC (MIni-halos in MIni-Clusters) project, focusing on Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, using LOFAR (54 MHz, 144 MHz), uGMRT (400 MHz, 650 MHz), and MeerKAT (1.28 GHz) data, as well as X-ray data. Chandra We detected diffuse radio emission in the central ∼100 kpc of both Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, spatially confined within the sloshing-induced cold fronts seen in X-ray images. The diffuse sources satisfy the classification criteria for radio mini-halos and represent the least powerful known to date, with 1.4 GHz radio powers of (2.2 W/Hz in Abell 496 and (1.3 W/Hz in ZwCl 235. The mini-halos have steep spectra (-1.9łeq In particular, in Abell 496, we find an outward steepening of the spectral index. In both clusters, the radio and X-ray surface brightness are correlated over the diffuse source extent, with sublinear or nearly linear slopes depending on frequency. Separately, we present the properties of two extended ($>200$ kpc) tailed radio galaxies in both clusters. The steep spectra, sublinear radio–X-ray correlations, and confinement within cold fronts suggest that contribution from fossil plasma advected from the central radio galaxy and plausible turbulent reacceleration are at play in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235. These two systems allow us to extend mini-halo scaling relations toward the low-power regime. We confirm a strong correlation between the mini-halo radio power and the cool core X-ray luminosity, with P_ 1.4 ∝ L_ X,70 ^ 1.5 . We find, for the first time, tentative indications that mini-halos with steeper radio spectra could preferentially be associated with lower core X-ray luminosities and lower radio power. We speculate that mini-halos may originate from a combination of hadronic and leptonic reacceleration mechanisms, whose relative importance varies with the properties of the host cluster: higher core X-ray luminosities at a given mass (i.e., reflecting higher gas densities) might make the contribution of hadronic interactions more substantial.

items.title: Development of Numerical Program on 2-Dimensional Inviscid Burgers Equation in Finite Volume Method with UPWIND and TVD Scheme
items.abstract: This paper presents the development and validation of a numerical solver for the two-dimensional steady-state inviscid Burgers equation using the Finite Volume Method (FVM). The Burgers equation serves as a fundamental model for studying nonlinear wave propagation and shock formation in hyperbolic conservation laws. Two numerical schemes are implemented and compared: the first-order Upwind scheme and high-resolution Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) schemes with various flux limiters including Min-Mod, Van Leer, Superbee, QUICK, and UMIST. The numerical solutions are validated against an exact analytical solution derived using the method of characteristics. Results demonstrate that while the Upwind scheme is robust and stable, it exhibits significant numerical diffusion that smears shock discontinuities. In contrast, TVD schemes achieve sharper shock resolution while maintaining monotonicity. The upwind scheme spreads the shock over 3.86 cells, whereas the limiters confine it to between 1.73 and 1.91 cells, reduce the L1 error by 60 to 67 per cent and reproduce the total variation of the exact solution exactly. Superbee gives the sharpest shock and QUICK the lowest L2 error, while Min-Mod is the most diffusive of the limiters; the most compressive limiters, however, only reach a steady state once the CFL number is reduced. A refinement study over nine grids gives observed orders of accuracy of 0.86 in L1 and 0.52 in L2 with a non-convergent maximum error, which is the behaviour expected of a first-order monotone scheme applied to a discontinuous solution.

items.title: Ensemble transport modelling of solar energetic particle events
items.abstract: Variations in the acceleration and transport conditions may account for the large inter-event variation noticed in observed solar energetic particle (SEP) events. As an initial attempt to quantify this variability, we examine the sensitivity of the solutions from a 2D SEP transport model to different initializations. An ensemble modeling approach is used to initiate the model with different input parameters, related to the acceleration and transport of these particles. We show that, at Earth’s position, seemingly small changes in the acceleration and transport parameters can lead to significant variations in the SEP peak intensity, onset delay, and peak delay. We posit that this might explain much of the observed SEP variability. While the methodology used in this work is a basic, first proof-of-concept, approach, we suggest that a similar, but refined, approach might be a viable method that could even be implemented in (near) real-time physics-based predictive models to illustrate the associated uncertainty in simulation results.

items.title: Galaxy Clusters from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. IV. Alignment of Member Galaxy Orientations at z < 0.5
items.abstract: Abstract Using DESI photometric catalog data, we systematically analyze the spatial alignment of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs) in clusters. The results reveal that, in both brightest central galaxy (BCG) alignment (BA) and satellite alignment (SA), the alignment signals of SFGs and QGs exhibit opposite trends in several aspects. For the BA signal, SFGs show stronger alignment in cluster outskirts, whereas QGs exhibit stronger alignment in inner regions. For the SA signal, both SFGs and QGs exhibit nearly isotropic signals in outer regions, while in inner regions they show opposite signals. In addition, the BA signal depends on cluster richness and QG fraction, and is more pronounced in mature clusters. Specifically, QGs show a stronger BA signal overall, which increases with luminosity and axis ratio, whereas SFGs show a weaker BA signal with no significant dependence on these parameters. The BA signal also exhibits a strong dependence on satellite galaxy color, which is independent of morphology. We confirm this by analyzing the BA signal in two populations: red disk and blue elliptical galaxies. However, neither BA nor SA shows a significant dependence on redshift at z < 0.5. In summary, these findings reflect how galaxy transport along cosmic filaments drives cluster evolution: early stage SFGs fall into clusters along filaments, and during cluster relaxation their spatial orientations are reshaped by gravitational potentials and tidal forces, weakening BA signal and enhancing SA signal. In contrast, QGs, as early cluster members, exhibit a more pronounced anisotropic distribution and maintain relatively stable spatial orientations.

items.title: A chemical inventory of the disk around the class 0 protostar L1527 IRS with ALMA
items.abstract: Planet formation starts in disks that are still embedded within their natal envelopes. Here, we compile an extensive inventory of the chemical composition of the disk and envelope ( < 3500 au) around the Class 0 protostar L1527 IRS. Using all publicly available ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) data, we report the detection of 40 molecules, including isotopologues. Of these, 23 are different molecular species and 29 are reported here for the first time toward L1527 in ALMA observations. CH 3 OH is the only complex organic molecule detected, while the hydrocarbon CH 3 CCH is the largest molecule detected. Overall, only a few programs are sensitive enough to detect emission unambiguously originating from the disk based on the kinematics. Nitrogen-bearing molecules are predominantly detected on more extended scales, while hydrocarbons show a distinct tail roughly along the southeastern outflow cavity wall, probably due to a stronger UV field in the eastern outflow lobe. The L1527 IRS protostellar system is not rich in sulfur-bearing molecules, with only strong emission observed for CS and SO. Overall, the envelope appears dominated by a carbon-rich chemistry, which seems to transition into an oxygen-rich chemistry in the disk. We calculate column densities of all detected species, providing a starting point to quantify the chemical diversity among young disks and the chemical evolution of the planet-forming material.

The "factory" was complete and operating efficiently, but then its primary supply was cut off. Had the nitrogen remained, life might have persisted on the surface of Mars to this day. This explains why the factory came to an abrupt halt, and why we find remnants of cells (such as in the ALH84001 meteorite) but no ongoing life. Why did the nitrogen disappear? items.title: The Making of Earth: From the first particle to a finished planet, element by element
items.abstract: Every atom in Earth was made somewhere else, at a particular time, by a particular process, and then sorted into its present place by a second sequence of events that took a few hundred million years. This paper tells both stories in order. The first runs over nine billion years: protons and neutrons in the first microseconds, hydrogen, helium and lithium in the first twenty minutes, the first atoms at 373,000 years, the first carbon, oxygen and iron in the first stars a hundred million years later, and then nine billion years of stellar generations in the Milky Way that built up the oxygen, magnesium, silicon and calcium of rock, the iron and nickel of the core, and the gold, platinum, uranium and thorium of the trace inventory. The second story begins 4,567.3 million years ago, when the first solids condensed from the cooling gas around the young Sun. It follows the condensation sequence that set which elements a rocky planet could hold, the growth of planetesimals heated by aluminium-26, the descent of iron into the core within about thirty million years, the Moon-forming impact, a magma ocean and steam atmosphere, the first oceans and continental crust by 4.4 billion years ago, the late addition of gold, platinum, water, carbon and nitrogen, the start of the geodynamo, and the radioactive heat engine that still drives the planet. A timeline (Figure 1, Table 2) and an element ledger (Table 3) record what arrived when and where it now resides. The arc is the history of the universe from creation to crunch in the Euler Cosmos, measured by the phase θₜ = H₀t, which runs from 0 at creation through 0.881 now to about 3.95 at the crunch. On the arc, Earth’s material is gathered by θₜ ≈ 0.59, and the planet is finished in outline by θₜ ≈ 0.62, before the first trace of life. Every number in the paper is imported from nuclear physics, astronomy, cosmochemistry and geology. The contribution is the ordering: a single continuous record from the first particle to a planet ready for chemistry.
