items.title: 4f-Electron-Regulated Dual-Periodic Bonding Evolution Across the Lanthanide Series.
items.abstract: Lanthanide-based catalysts have attracted increasing attention due to their unique electronic structures, yet the relationship between 4f electron evolution and catalytic behavior remains unclear. Here, using structurally uniform lanthanide single-atom catalysts as a model platform, we systematically investigate the influence of 4f electron filling on bonding evolution across the lanthanide series. We reveal a dual-periodic trend in lanthanide-support binding energies and adsorbate bonding energies, which increases from La to Eu and from Gd to Yb. This behavior originates from progressive electron redistribution between 5d and 4f orbitals, which modulates the electron population of bonding orbitals. The half-filled 4f 7 configuration induces an abrupt transition between Eu and Gd. Furthermore, similar crystal-field splitting enables robust linear relationships between binding and bonding energies across diverse coordination environments. More importantly, the persistence of these electronic characteristics across diverse coordination environments demonstrates that the dual-periodic evolution represents an intrinsic feature of lanthanide chemistry rather than a system-specific phenomenon. These findings establish a 4f-electron-regulated bonding framework for understanding lanthanide reactivity and guiding catalyst design.

items.title: Analysis of the phylogenetic position of Pseudexorchis Yamaguti, 1938 (Digenea: Opisthorchioidea) suggests new complexity in the relationships of the Cryptogonimidae.
items.abstract: Pseudexorchis Yamaguti, 1938 is a genus of opisthorchioid digeneans, which is currently classified as a member of the Heterophyidae. Only one species is recognised in this genus, Pseudexorchis major (Hasegawa, 1935), which parasitises freshwater silurid fishes as adults. The aim of this study is to evaluate the family affiliation of Pseudexorchis based on phylogenetic data. We obtained the sequences of several genetic markers from a single adult specimen of P. major ex Silurus asotus Linnaeus, 1758 from Japan, which allowed us to identify it as a member of a phylogenetic lineage previously named by Miura and Takisawa (2024) as Type B. The lineage Type B appeared as a sister to P. major Type A of Miura and Takisawa (2024). The degree of genetic differentiation between Type B and Type A, mainly based on the cox1 gene partial sequence, allows us to hypothesise the species status of these lineages. The trees based on 28S rRNA, 28S rRNA + ITS2 , and ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 datasets were most informative for phylogenetic inferences. In our analyses, Pseudexorchis was clustered with cryptogonimids Acanthostomum yahuarcaquense Cajiao-Mora and Bullard in Cajiao-Mora, Brule, Dutton, Caicedo-Portilla, and Bullard, 2025, Neocladocystis spp., Tanganyikatrema spp., and the nonugens KC489791 and KC489792 ( 28S rRNA-tree ), or only A. yahuarcaquense (28S rRNA + ITS2-tree), or Acanthostomum cf. americanum (Pérez-Vigueras, 1956) (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-tree); the clade of these species was closer to the clade formed by opisthorchids and heterophyids than to other cryptogonimids. Thus, the presented data do not support the hypothesis that Pseudexorchis belongs to the Heterophyidae and demonstrate paraphyly of the Cryptogonimidae.

items.title: Effects of predator recovery and climate change on the long-term demography of a flagship herbivore.
items.abstract: Large herbivores play important roles in ecosystems across the globe, but limitations to study and inference have left gaps in predictive theories of their population dynamics, particularly following carnivore recoveries. Studies using spatial variation have explored the broad patterns of top-down and bottom-up forces in large herbivores. However, temporal changes in a population provide the most direct evidence for predicting future effects, and long-term studies spanning variation in top-down and bottom-up forces remain rare. We used 36 years of data on elk (Cervus canadensis) in the western United States in an integrated population model to test the effects of top-down (Puma concolor recovery) and bottom-up (drought) forces on pregnancy rates and age-based survival across a range of elk densities in the context of human harvest. We then quantified the proportion of variance in population growth attributable to those forces relative to the influences of harvest, age structure and unmodelled variation in demographic rates. Both top-down and bottom-up forces had measurable effects on elk population dynamics, with puma recovery reducing survival in the first 2 years of life and drought reducing pregnancy probability and survival at all ages. We also found negative density dependence in pregnancy, consistent with bottom-up control and positive density dependence in survival of young, consistent with predator swamping. Harvest explained the greatest proportion of variation in population growth (26%). Of the non-harvest parameters, drought severity had the largest effect, explaining as much variation (16%) as all of the unmodelled changes in demographic rates. Puma recovery explained 13% of the variation, and density dependence explained 8%. Without more long-term studies spanning sufficient ecological variation, the predictive abilities of large herbivore ecology will remain limited. With ongoing anthropogenic changes to the forces acting on large herbivores around the world, improving predictions will be invaluable to conservation.

items.title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures.
items.abstract: Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. As major food-producing animals with frequent human contact, cattle represent a critical host at the human-animal interface; however, the early-life establishment of their respiratory virome and its evolutionary connections to viruses from other hosts remain underexplored. Here, we longitudinally profile the upper respiratory tract (URT) virome of beef calves from birth to weaning using an optimized viral enrichment procedure and metagenomic workflow. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.

items.title: Heterologous expression of the Metarhizium anisopliae barc gene cluster reveals a diphenyl ether-to-xanthene transformation in barceloneic acid biosynthesis.
items.abstract: Filamentous fungi generate chemical diversity through several evolutionary strategies, including the elaboration of conserved biosynthetic intermediates into structurally distinct secondary metabolites. Emodin and its corresponding anthrone are central intermediates in fungal aromatic polyketide metabolism, yet the enzymatic logic that remodels these precursors into more complex scaffolds remains incompletely understood. To investigate this process, we examined an infection-responsive non-reducing polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster ( barc ) from the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae predicted to encode an emodin-derived aromatic polyketide pathway. Heterologous reconstruction of the barc cluster in Aspergillus nidulans led to the production of the previously reported diphenyl ether barceloneic acid A (1) and the xanthene barceloneic acid C2 (2), together with two new compounds derived from 2, barceloneic acids D and E (3 and 4). Compound 3 is a cyclopentanone adduct of the xanthene 2, whereas 4 is a polyketide-indole hybrid, highlighting the chemical reactivity of the xanthene 2 scaffold. Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2. This defines a previously uncharacterised oxidative scaffold-remodelling step in barceloneic acid biosynthesis, revealing how an emodin-derived pathway can access a xanthene scaffold. Deletion of the backbone gene barcB in M. anisopliae did not significantly alter virulence towards Tenebrio molitor (mealworm) under the conditions tested, suggesting that barceloneic acids are not essential for pathogenicity in this insect model.

items.title: Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) nymphs demonstrate robust jumping and gripping performance following limb loss.
items.abstract: The spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is an invasive hemipteran spreading across the USA. Eradication campaigns, such as 'See It, Squish It', rely on mechanical elimination. However, lanternflies often escape by executing hindlimb-driven leaps. Although escape rates remain unquantified, the physical nature of these eradication attempts likely results in individuals surviving with damaged/missing limbs. Lanternflies do not exhibit limb autotomy, and it remains unclear how well they tolerate injury. To evaluate the effects of limb loss on locomotor performance, we amputated a single forelimb, midlimb or hindlimb in lanternfly nymphs and measured three ecologically relevant metrics: jumping and climbing velocity and pull strength. We also tracked recovery over several days post-amputation for jumping and climbing trials. Jumping velocity and pull strength were unaffected by limb removal. In contrast, climbing velocity declined significantly across all groups, with the greatest reductions observed following forelimb and hindlimb removal. This decrease in climbing velocity was associated with changes in both stride length and stride frequency. However, because climbing velocity also declined in the control group, it remains unclear whether limb amputation alone - or the intervention itself - was responsible for these effects. No evidence of performance recovery was observed over time. These findings demonstrate the fault-tolerant nature of the lanternfly locomotor system, likely supported by mechanical redundancy and decentralized neuromuscular control. The ability to maintain essential behaviors following limb loss may represent a complementary evolutionary strategy to autotomy, centered on resilience rather than pre-programed limb sacrifice. This performance robustness likely contributes to the lanternfly's invasive success.

items.title: Propofol Modulates Fear Memory Reconsolidation by Inhibiting D2 Receptor-Expressing Neurons in the Medial Prefrontal Cortex.
items.abstract: Fear memory reconsolidation provides a temporal window for modifying established fear memories, yet the underlying cellular and neural circuit mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using in vivo fiber photometry and chemogenetic approaches in freely moving mice, we show that propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation by inhibiting D2 receptor-expressing neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). These neurons exhibit heightened activity during fear memory reconsolidation and project prominently to the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Notably, local pharmacological activation of D2 receptors in the mPFC recapitulates the fear-attenuating effect of propofol when administered during the reconsolidation window. Circuit-level investigations further show that propofol suppresses the reconsolidation-associated enhancement of the mPFC D2 -BLA synaptic transmission, and chemogenetic activation of this projection counteracts the effect of propofol on fear memory reconsolidation. Moreover, selective knockdown of D2 receptors in BLA-projecting mPFC neurons diminishes the effect of propofol, supporting a critical role for D2 receptor signaling within this projection-defined circuit. Together, these findings identify the mPFC D2 -BLA circuit as a key neural substrate through which propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation and highlight prefrontal D2 receptor signaling as a potential target for reconsolidation-based interventions aimed at maladaptive fear memories.

items.title: Only Your Mind Sets the Limits: Socio-Cognitive Pathways between Growth Mindset and Reading Achievement Across Nordic and Chinese Educational Systems.
items.abstract: Background Mindset theory has increasingly shifted from asking whether growth mindsets predict achievement to asking how, for whom, and under what conditions beliefs about intelligence become motivationally consequential. Aims This study contributes to that theoretical shift by examining mindset as a distal belief embedded within a broader social-cognitive system of achievement motivation. Sample and methods Using PISA 2018 data on 36,905 15-year-old students in Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Hong Kong, and Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang, China, we modeled associations among mindset, socioeconomic background, mastery goals, motivation to master school tasks, reading self-concept, general self-efficacy, fear of failure, and reading achievement through a multi-group path analysis approach. Results Model results showed that a growth mindset was positively associated with reading achievement in the Nordic countries, unrelated to achievement in Hong Kong, and negatively associated with achievement in B-S-J-Z China. Indirect effects were generally small, while reading self-concept emerged as the most consistent proximal correlate of achievement. These patterns suggest that mindset is best understood not as a universal predictor of achievement but as a context-sensitive component within culturally situated socio-cognitive systems. Conclusions The study, therefore, uses cross-national evidence to refine the theoretical placement of mindset within achievement motivation, highlighting the importance of mechanisms, proximal competence beliefs, and cultural boundary conditions.

items.title: Prospective Associations Between Emotion Dysregulation, Problematic Internet Use, Internalizing Symptoms, and Life Satisfaction: A Baseline-Adjusted Two-Wave Study of Polish Adults.
items.abstract: Longitudinal evidence remains limited on whether the association between problematic Internet use (PIU) and life satisfaction persists after accounting for prior PIU, internalizing symptoms, and life satisfaction. This study examined whether baseline emotion regulation difficulties prospectively predicted PIU, depressive and generalized anxiety symptoms, and life satisfaction 6 months later. Participants were 2,122 Polish adults aged 19-98 years; 1,412 completed follow-up. All constructs were assessed at both waves. Baseline-adjusted path models used 50 multiply imputed datasets. Baseline emotion dysregulation predicted higher PIU (β = 0.155, 95 percent confidence interval [CI] [0.107, 0.204], p < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms at follow-up. Within T2, PIU was positively associated with internalizing symptoms, which were negatively associated with life satisfaction; direct PIU-life satisfaction paths were negligible (depressive symptoms: β = 0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.035, 0.042], p = 0.846; generalized anxiety symptoms: β = 0.002, 95 percent CI [-0.037, 0.041], p = 0.926). The serial indirect associations were statistically significant but very small: depressive symptoms, β = -0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.006, -0.002], p < 0.001; generalized anxiety symptoms, β = -0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.006, -0.001], p = 0.002. Reciprocal prospective sensitivity models showed small PIU-to-symptom associations but no prospective PIU-to-life-satisfaction association. Other sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the findings. The findings highlight the contribution of internalizing symptoms to the PIU-life satisfaction association after baseline adjustment, but same-wave indirect pathways do not establish temporal mediation or intervention benefits.

items.title: Disordered Eating Symptom Profiles in Low-Income, Racially Minoritized Adults.
items.abstract: Eating disorder (ED) research has traditionally assumed that symptoms cluster in the same way across populations. If this assumption is incorrect, models and assessment tools developed with advantaged samples may miss substantial symptom burden in marginalized populations. We investigated, for the first time, how ED symptoms cluster in racially minoritized, low-income adults. We used latent profile analysis to identify empirically derived ED symptom profiles in an intersectionally marginalized sample of women and men living in Detroit (N = 561; 87.5% Black; modal annual income < $10,000). We then applied BCH estimation to examine how demographic factors (age, sex, racial identity, and body mass index [BMI]) related to profile membership. The best-fitting model included seven profiles, some of which meaningfully differed from existing ED diagnostic categories and clinical heuristics. For example, two elevated symptom profiles were predominantly male, and participants in the profiles with the highest levels of restraint also had the highest BMIs. The highest levels of binge eating were observed in participants with relatively low co-occurring restraint. The most acute symptom profile was characterized by high body dissatisfaction, anxiety, depression, and restraint due to both monetary and weight/shape concerns. Disordered eating may present differently in disadvantaged populations, with decoupling of mechanisms that are more tightly linked in relatively advantaged settings (e.g., binge eating and restraint). Co-occurring restraint due to monetary and weight/shape concerns appears to be common, highlighting the importance of attending to multiple drivers of disordered eating in individuals from marginalized backgrounds.

items.title: What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
items.abstract: The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.

items.title: Neural, vascular, motor and autonomic habituation to high-intensity auditory stimulation: A multimodal characterization of the human defensive responses.
items.abstract: The defense reflex has been extensively characterized across sensory modalities; however, the integration of electrical, neurovascular, motor, and peripheral autonomic responses involving the central and autonomic nervous systems remains poorly understood. This study investigated defensive responses to high-intensity auditory stimulation using a multimodal approach combining electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and peripheral physiological measures. Participants were exposed to twenty white-noise bursts (100 dB, 500 ms, instantaneous rise time) separated by silent intervals (50 ± 10 s), grouped into five blocks to assess initial responses and habituation. Hemodynamic responses revealed widespread activation of bilateral auditory and frontal regions following stimulus onset, with a progressive reduction in response amplitude and extension of active channels across blocks. Network analysis suggests progressive reorganization of functional connectivity between sensory and frontal regions across repeated stimulation. At the peripheral level, habituation was observed in phasic electrodermal activity, vascular indices, motor response, EEG-derived ocular activity, and parasympathetic cardiac modulation, primarily after the first block, whereas respiratory measures remained stable. Cardiac defense-like responses show a multi-temporal component structure, with habituation restricted to the late decelerative phase. Multivariate analyses revealed a structured yet partially independent organization of neural and autonomic responses to habituation. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive characterization of multisystem responses to intense auditory stimulation, highlighting selective habituation across central, neurovascular, motor, and autonomic systems, and offering new insights into how neurovascular and peripheral processes adapt to repeated auditory threats.

items.title: Ligand-specific effects of 5-HT2A receptor antagonists on fear extinction in C57BL/6J mice: Comparative insights from MDL 11,939 and MDL 100,907.
items.abstract: Serotonin (5-HT) 2A receptors (5-HT 2 AR) modulate corticolimbic circuits underlying fear extinction, but the behavioral consequences of 5-HT 2 AR antagonism during extinction remain poorly defined. Here, we examined the systemic effects of the 5-HT 2 A/ 2 C antagonist MDL 11,939 (Glemanserin) and the selective 5-HT 2 A antagonist MDL 100,907 (Volinanserin) on fear extinction in adult female and male C57BL/6J mice. Prior to drug administration, mice acquired comparable conditioned freezing responses during delay fear conditioning. Twenty-four hours later, acute administration of MDL 11,939 (1.0 mg/kg) or MDL 100,907 (0.01 mg/kg) increased freezing to the first conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation on Extinction Day 1 in males, indicating enhanced expression of conditioned fear. Repeated administration of MDL 11,939 significantly impaired extinction in male mice, evidenced by increased freezing across extinction trials and an increased number of trials required to reach extinction criterion. Neither acute nor repeated MDL 11,939 altered extinction in female mice. In males, MDL 100,907 produced a transient increase in freezing during extinction but did not delay extinction acquisition and had no effect in females. Because MDL 11,939 has reported affinity for 5-HT 2 C receptors, we tested potential contributions of 5-HT 2 C receptor antagonism in a separate cohort of male mice given repeated administration of the selective 5-HT 2 C antagonist SB 242084 (0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg). Neither dose affected conditioned fear expression, extinction learning, or trials required to reach extinction criterion. Together, these findings demonstrate ligand-, sex-, and dose-dependent effects of 5-HT 2 AR antagonism on fear extinction and suggest that distinct intracellular receptor signaling mechanisms may differentially regulate extinction-related behavior.

items.title: Simultaneous brain-spinal fMRI reveals neural mechanisms of TENS-induced analgesia.
items.abstract: Introduction Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) can produce analgesia, but its associated cortical, brainstem, and spinal response patterns in humans remain incompletely understood. Objectives To compare the analgesic effects and associated brain-spinal response patterns of two TENS protocols: high-frequency/low-intensity and low-frequency/high-intensity stimulation. Methods Ninety-two healthy adults were randomized to high-frequency TENS, low-frequency TENS, or sham stimulation. Bilateral heat-pain responses were assessed using simultaneous brain-spinal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) before and after a 30-min intervention. Pain ratings, regional activation, and periaqueductal gray (PAG)-centered functional connectivity were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with correction for multiple comparisons. Results The two TENS protocols produced different spatial profiles of analgesia. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced treated-side analgesia relative to sham for pain intensity (β = -2.57, 95 % confidence interval [CI] [-3.26, -1.87]) and unpleasantness (β = -2.53, 95 % CI [-3.51, -1.55]). Treated-side analgesia was accompanied by reduced heat-evoked activity in the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), PAG, rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), and C6 spinal cord, increased ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity, and altered PAG-spinal connectivity. Low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia, reducing pain intensity on the treated and untreated sides (β = -2.07 and -1.75, respectively) and unpleasantness (β = -1.98 and -1.70, respectively). This bilateral effect was accompanied by reduced activity in primary somatosensory cortex (S1)/dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)/supplementary motor area (SMA), S2, and spinal cord, together with PAG-S1 and PAG-spinal connectivity changes. Conclusion TENS analgesia was associated with protocol-specific brain-spinal response patterns. High-frequency/low-intensity TENS produced localized analgesia with neural changes consistent with spinal and supraspinal modulation, whereas low-frequency/high-intensity TENS produced bilateral analgesia with broader PAG-sensorimotor-spinal involvement.

items.title: Charitable giving with earned and windfall money: behavioral and ERP responses to donation-risk information.
items.abstract: Charitable giving depends both on how money is acquired and on expectations about its eventual use. However, it remains unclear how monetary source shapes the evaluation of donation-risk information after a donation decision. Twenty-six participants made repeated donation decisions using earned and windfall money while electroencephalography was recorded. After each choice, a cue indicated a 70 % probability of allocation to either a lower-credibility charity (high risk) or a higher-credibility charity (low risk). One decision and its associated allocation rule were implemented at the end of the experiment. Participants donated more from windfall than earned money and reported greater regret and lower satisfaction after high-risk than low-risk cues. Mixed-effects analysis also showed lower next-trial donations following high-risk cues. Windfall money was associated with less positive frontocentral mean voltage within the feedback-related negativity (FRN) interval, whereas low-risk information elicited a larger P3. The predicted monetary-source-by-risk interaction was not supported, and Bayesian comparisons favored the zero-interaction model over the specified alternative. These findings show that monetary acquisition context and prospective allocation information both matter for charitable giving and its neural evaluation. They extend research on donation-related feedback by demonstrating behavioral adjustment to consequential risk information before the recipient and the realized charitable outcome are known.

items.title: Perceived descriptive norms and actual rates of contraception and fertility discussion among adults in rural Uganda: a whole-population study.
items.abstract: Objectives Women in Uganda face challenges in meeting their reproductive needs. Communication about contraception is one pathway through which couples navigate these challenges. However, it is unknown how often discussions occur among couples and whether perceptions of others' discussion behavior shape discussion frequency. We examined associations between individuals' beliefs about how often peer couples discuss contraception and fertility intentions and frequency of personal discussion. Study design We collected data from all partnered adults of reproductive age living in a single parish in southwestern Uganda as part of a larger study focused on social connection and health. Participants reported how frequently they discussed contraception decisions and fertility intentions with a partner, and how often most other reproductive-aged couples in their village discussed these topics (i.e., perceived norms). We compared perceptions to reported communication frequency aggregated at the village level, and we used sex-stratified multivariable Poisson regression models with robust estimates of variance to estimate the association between personal behavior and perceived norms. Results Of 908 participants (92% response rate), 560 (62%) frequently discussed contraception decisions and fertility intentions, 174 (19%) rarely did, and 174 (19%) never did. Regarding perceptions, 305 (34%) incorrectly thought most others rarely or never discussed these topics and 197 (22%) said they did not know. Individuals who did not know or who thought discussions rarely or never occurred were less likely to discuss these topics compared to individuals who accurately perceived the norm (e.g., among women, adjusted relative risk for not knowing the norm=0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61-0.91; p-value =0.003). Conclusions Inaccurate beliefs about local discussion norms were associated with a lower likelihood of personally discussing contraception and fertility intentions. Emphasizing actual rates of discussions through public messaging or through existing intervention strategies (e.g., couples-based counselling) might motivate discussions within couples and support reproductive autonomy.

items.title: Longitudinal associations among psychophysical factors, biobehavioral vulnerabilities and pain-related outcomes following acute musculoskeletal injury in adolescents.
items.abstract: Up to 30% of adolescents with acute musculoskeletal (MSK) injuries develop chronic pain. Research has increasingly focused on identification of risk factors associated with outcomes following acute injury; however, prospective longitudinal studies examining both psychophysical and biobehavioral factors beyond short-term follow-up are limited in adolescents. The current study used mixed effects models (MEM) to test longitudinal associations among biobehavioral factors (e.g., sleep disturbances, anxiety and depressive symptoms, pain-related cognitions and behaviors), psychophysical responses (e.g., conditioned pain modulation, temporal summation) and pain-related outcomes (pain intensity, pain-related disability and quality of life; QOL) over one year following acute MSK injury. Participants were 226 adolescents 11-17 years (and one parent) participating in a prospective longitudinal study with data collected via self-report, actigraphy and quantitative sensory testing (QST) at three timepoints (< 30 days, 3 months, 12 months post-injury). Results of MEM revealed within and between-person associations among psychological factors and pain-related disability and QOL. Sleep duration (within-person effect) and pain-related cognitions and behaviors (between-person effect) were associated with pain intensity. Pain-related cognitions and behaviors were also associated with pain-related disability (between-person effect) and QOL (within and between-person effects). Temporal summation (TS) was the only psychophysical factor associated with pain outcomes (between-person effect) with higher average TS associated with higher pain intensity. Findings point to the relatively stronger influence of biobehavioral (versus psychophysical) factors as responsive indicators of adolescents' recovery trajectories and suggest targeted interventions may be directed at general anxiety and depressive symptoms, pain-specific cognitions and behaviors, and sleep to improve outcomes. PERSPECTIVE: This article presents results of a longitudinal multi-method study examining pain-related outcomes in adolescents following musculoskeletal injury. Findings point to the influence of biobehavioral factors in the longer-term recovery period and suggest potential importance of interventions targeting general anxiety and depressive symptoms, pain-specific cognitions and behaviors, and sleep in adolescents post musculoskeletal injury.

items.title: Elaborative processing before retrieval practice enhances semantic organization and long-term memory.
items.abstract: One longstanding goal in psychology is to identify more effective ways of learning. Recent work has shown that elaborative processing can amplify the memory benefits of retrieval practice, yet the mechanisms underlying this advantage remain unclear. Using electroencephalography (EEG), the present study examined how elaborative processing before retrieval practice influences later memory and encoding-related neural processing and representations, relative to context processing. Behaviorally, memory performance was better for elaborative processing plus retrieval practice than for context processing plus retrieval practice. During the first encoding phase, elaborative processing elicited a more negative N400, whereas context processing elicited a more positive LPC. Moreover, the N400 and LPC differences between elaborative and context processing during encoding were significantly correlated with the corresponding differences in 7-day recognition performance. Representational similarity analyses further showed stronger semantic-category organization and greater representational reorganization across repeated encoding under elaborative processing than under context processing. These findings suggest that elaborative processing before retrieval practice enhances long-term memory and is associated with broader semantic processing and stronger semantic organization during encoding. More broadly, the results suggest that richer connections with pre-existing semantic knowledge may be one way in which encoding variability supports long-term memory.

items.title: Prospective Associations Between Older Adults' Social Connections and Trajectories of Change in Physical Activity and Psychological Well-Being During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Parallel Process Approach.
items.abstract: Associations between seven social connection trajectories and changes in physical activity (PA) and psychological well-being were examined among older adults (N = 890, Mage = 65.05 years, SD = 6.91) during the COVID-19 pandemic. Six online monthly surveys were administered between October 2021 and May 2022. Latent growth curve modeling demonstrated injunctive and descriptive norms did not change over time. Social network, relatedness, stress, and negative affect decreased, and social support quantity and quality increased over time. Social participation, positive affect, and light-intensity PA changed quadratically, and moderate to vigorous PA increased steadily and then slowed over time. Changes in social participation, social network, and social support were positively associated with changes in moderate to vigorous PA and psychological well-being. Findings support theories suggesting social connections play a dynamic, multidimensional role in health behaviors and highlight the need for future research examining how social connections contribute to higher intensity PA and well-being among older adults.

items.title: Motor inhibition and impulsivity in alcohol use disorder and at-risk drinking: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Harmful alcohol use is a global health problem, with deficits in impulse control, encompassing motor inhibition and motor impulsivity, associated with its development and persistence. We aimed to synthesise performance-based motor inhibition and self-reported impulsivity in individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD) and at-risk drinkers, relative to controls, and to compare the two alcohol-use groups. Pre-registered systematic review and subgroup meta-analysis. PubMed, PsycINFO, EMBASE, MEDLINE and CINAHL were searched to 31 December 2024, supplemented by reference-list searching and snowballing. Adults with diagnosed AUD or at-risk drinking were compared with healthy or low-severity drinking controls across 110 independent datasets. Impulse control was measured using performance-based motor inhibition tasks (go/no-go and stop-signal tasks) and self-report motor impulsivity questionnaires (Barratt Impulsiveness Scale; BIS). Primary outcomes were go/no-go commission errors, stop-signal reaction time and BIS total and motor scores. The combined alcohol-use group exhibited poorer motor inhibition than controls on go/no-go commission errors [g = -0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI) = -0.43 to -0.11] and stop-signal reaction time (g = -0.20, 95% CI = -0.36 to -0.05); and higher self-reported Barratt total (g = -0.77, 95% CI = -0.97 to -0.58) and motor impulsivity scores (g = -0.68, 95% CI = -0.80 to -0.55). Individuals with AUD reported higher impulsivity than at-risk drinkers on Barratt total and motor scores (P < 0.001 and P = 0.022, respectively). The AUD and at-risk groups did not differ significantly in stop-signal reaction time (P = 0.247), whereas the commission-error effect was larger among at-risk drinkers (P = 0.033). Alcohol use disorder and at-risk drinking appear to be associated with poorer performance-based inhibition and higher self-reported impulsivity compared with healthy or low-severity drinking, with consistently larger effects on self-reported impulsivity. Unexpectedly, the two alcohol groups (alcohol use disorder and at-risk drinking) in this study were better differentiated by self-reported motor impulsivity than by performance-based motor-inhibition measures.

items.title: Substance-free and substance-related reinforcement in relation to substance use: A meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Contemporary behavioral economic theory conceptualizes addiction as an operant reinforcer pathology in which substance use is substantively influenced by reinforcement obtained through substance-free sources. The aim of the current meta-analysis was to quantitatively synthesize cross-sectional associations between both substance-related and substance-free reinforcement in relation to substance use and substance-related problems. Systematic bibliographic searches were conducted in PubMed and PsychINFO from 1998 to 20 March 2026. Main eligibility criteria included human, peer-reviewed studies that measured substance use, the reinforcement ratio (proportionate substance-related reinforcement), substance-related reinforcement and/or substance-free reinforcement, which yielded 28 studies and 31 samples. Pearson's r correlations were extracted for the reinforcement ratio, substance-related reinforcement and substance-free reinforcement in relation to substance use problem/severity and quantity/frequency outcomes. Six random effects meta-analyses were conducted based on these key variables, with an average aggregated sample size of n = 5663 (range = 4344-7258). The reinforcement ratio (RR) and substance-related reinforcement (SR) were statistically significantly associated with both substance use problem/severity [RR r = 0.33, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.27-0.39, number of effect estimates (k) = 19, I2 = 85.06, SR r = 0.34, 95% CI = 0.29-0.60, k = 12, I2 = 94.28, Ps < 0.001] and quantity/frequency (RR r = 0.38, 95% CI = 0.31-0.46, k = 17, I2 = 86.22, SR r = 0.34, 95% CI = 0.25-0.43, k = 10, I2 = 87.99, Ps < 0.001). Substance-free reinforcement was statistically significantly negatively associated with quantity/frequency (r = -0.11, 95% CI = -0.17 to -0.04, k = 13, I2 = 81.57, P = 0.002) but not problem/severity of substance use (r = -0.07, 95% CI = -0.14 to 0.00, k = 16, I2 = 83.38, P = 0.051). Continuous study moderators (% male, % White, study year) and categorical study moderators (reinforcement measurement tool) explained some heterogeneity across analyses. Overall, there was minimal evidence of publication bias. Substance-related reinforcement and the reinforcement ratio appear to be moderately strong correlates of substance problems/severity and quantity/frequency outcomes.

items.title: Understanding children's "tinkering" in innovative problem-solving: The roles of knowledge integration, relational reasoning, and design stance.
items.abstract: A key feature of human societies is the presence of technological traditions. Different cultural groups develop and impart a vast array of problem-solving methods to future generations that are suited for their living environment and cultural lifestyle. Central to this process is our capacity for innovative problem-solving to generate adaptive solutions. The extant developmental psychology literature has focused on invention and novel idea generation, typically assessed empirically using tool making, tool use, and divergent thinking tasks, and focusing on the end product of innovation (creative invention) and goal attainment. Yet, we still know little about the iterative process of 'tinkering' that involves purposeful exploration and experimentation of possible combinations of sub-components leading up to an innovative end product. In light of recent evidence, we propose that 'tinkering' plays a pivotal role in children's capacity for tool innovation and that further exploration of the development of this process is warranted. In this article, we suggest additional cognitive mechanisms that underpin tinkering behaviors: the ability to evaluate and integrate knowledge, along with relational and abstraction reasoning, and the design stance. We hope this proposal spurs additional work for exploring the cognitive foundations for developing innovative problem-solving.

items.title: Executive functions and gait in sedentary versus frequently jogging adults: Evidence from a dual-task paradigm.
items.abstract: Background Executive functions and gait are highly associated and can have positive spill-over effects. While there is some evidence that the type of sport and exercise-related skills can influence these crossover benefits of executive functions and gait, most studies have compared open-skill and closed-skill sports, emphasizing the benefits to open-skill sports which are highly adaptive and less predictable. Limited research has examined the unique cognitive and motor benefits of closed-skill sports, or more predictable forms of exercise with limited movement sets, such as jogging or swimming, particularly when compared to sedentary people. Methodology Therefore, the present study examined gait during executive functioning dual-task performance for inhibition, switching, and working memory domains with and without concurrent walking among N = 65 adults with either high rates of physical activity via closed-skill sports (i.e., jogging) or limited rates of physical activity (i.e., sedentary group). Results Overall, significant performance declines from the single- to dual-task were present in average accuracy and gait variability across the entire sample, with only subtle group differences in executive functions, favoring the joggers. Cognitive and motor dual-task costs (DTCs) were only descriptively and not significantly worse in the sedentary group. Interpretation Broad reductions from the single- to dual-task conditions revealed consistent cognitive-motor interference in the entire sample. Few differences between joggers and sedentary adults likely support the age-stabilization of cognitive-motor skills in young adulthood.

items.title: Words under the skin: Physiological responses to interoceptive metaphors.
items.abstract: Embodied accounts of language propose that linguistic meaning is grounded in sensorimotor systems. While previous research has focused on the central nervous system, the involvement of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) in language comprehension remains underexplored. To fill this gap, we investigated whether processing interoceptive metaphors, namely figurative expressions referring to internal bodily sensations (e.g., 'I feel butterflies in my stomach'), modulates the ANS. Forty-five healthy participants read interoceptive metaphors and non-bodily-related literal sentences while cardiac, electrodermal, and respiratory signals were continuously recorded. We further distinguished between two types of interoceptive metaphors, depending on whether the interoceptive element served as the target (INT-target, e.g., 'I feel butterflies in my stomach') or source domain (INT-source, e.g., 'I thirst for success' to convey ambition) of the metaphor. Results revealed subtle but measurable effects: compared to non-bodily-related literal sentences, interoceptive metaphors were associated with higher heart rate variability and longer inspiratory duration. No significant differences emerged between INT-target and INT-source metaphors. These findings provide the first evidence that language grounded in internal bodily experience is associated with subtle differences in selected autonomic indices relative to non-bodily-related literal sentences.

items.title: Working- and long-term memory target templates converge to produce coactive guidance of attention during visual search.
items.abstract: Templates that guide attention during visual search can be maintained in visual working memory (VWM) or in long-term memory (LTM). A central challenge for theories of attention is explaining how these sources of bias combine to determine selection. Here, we tested whether they converge on a common priority signal. Specifically, we contrasted a coactive model of guidance, assuming convergence, with three non-coactive alternatives, each holding that guidance from VWM and LTM operate independently. Participants searched for the presence of a target defined by either of two cued colors. One cued color changed on each trial (dynamic, engaging VWM), whereas the other remained constant (static, engaging LTM). The target could match either one of the cued colors (single-target trials) or both (redundant-target trials). Through distributional analysis, we tested for the presence of redundant-target RTs that were faster than could have been generated by the two individual guidance processes operating independently in parallel. Such "violations" of the race model inequality (RMI) are observed only within a coactive system. For single-target trials, searches were substantially more efficient for dynamic-match targets than for static-match targets. Nevertheless, we observed robust violations of the RMI on redundant-target trials. Together, these results demonstrate that target templates can be maintained in qualitatively different states yet ultimately converge to jointly influence a common attentional priority signal.

items.title: Cortisol and mental health in the perinatal period: A systematic review of maternal, infant, and dyadic associations.
items.abstract: The perinatal period is a critical window for maternal and infant mental health, during which stress physiology may influence psychological and developmental outcomes. Cortisol, the end product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, is widely used as a biomarker of stress regulation, although its relationship with mental health in mother-infant dyads remains unclear. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Four electronic databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between January 2015 and March 2025, resulting in 27 studies that met the inclusion criteria. This systematic review examined the associations between cortisol and mental health during the perinatal period, focusing on maternal psychological functioning, infant socioemotional outcomes, mother-infant physiological synchrony, and the potential influence of maternal cortisol on later infant development. The findings indicate that associations between cortisol and mental health are complex and context dependent. Maternal cortisol was linked to symptoms of depression, anxiety, and trauma, although studies reported heterogeneous patterns. Infant cortisol was associated with maternal psychological distress, caregiving experiences, and socioemotional functioning, but findings varied across contexts and developmental stages. Evidence from dyadic studies suggested physiological coupling between mothers and infants, supporting the idea that stress regulation processes may be transmitted across generations. Some studies also indicated that maternal cortisol during pregnancy may be related to later infant physiological and behavioral outcomes, although results were not consistent. Overall, cortisol appears to provide valuable information about stress regulation during the perinatal period, but current evidence does not support its use as a specific biomarker of perinatal mental health. Instead, the findings support a biopsychosocial perspective in which cortisol reflects the dynamic interplay among biological stress regulation, maternal psychological functioning, caregiving experiences, and the broader relational environment. Further longitudinal and dyadic research is needed to clarify the mechanisms linking stress physiology and mental health in mothers and infants.

items.title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning.
items.abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning, sometimes benefitting learning and other times making it more challenging. However, all prior studies investigating effects of talker variability have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used a novel active learning paradigm wherein 3- and 4-year old preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, but that talker variability does not predict word learning. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children do seek out variability, but that word learning outcomes are most predicted by their relative vocabulary sizes and not talker variability choices. These results inform theories on the roles of both talker variability and active learning in language learning.

items.title: Prefrontal rTMS modulates dynamic expectancy processes to shape subsequent pain experience.
items.abstract: Pain expectancy is a major determinant of pain perception, and identifying effective approaches to modulate expectancy may provide new opportunities for pain intervention. High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) has been implicated in expectancy-related pain modulation. However, it remains unclear how DLPFC-rTMS influences distinct stages of expectancy processing and how these changes relate to subsequent pain experience. Thirty-three healthy participants completed a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover study. Participants received real or sham high-frequency DLPFC-rTMS and performed a pain expectancy paradigm before and after stimulation while EEG was recorded. The paradigm dissociated expectancy formation and maintenance under certain and uncertain predictive contexts. Behaviorally, DLPFC-rTMS reduced pain intensity and unpleasantness, accompanied by a reduction in expected pain, and mediation analysis identified an indirect effect through expected pain. At the neural level, DLPFC-rTMS increased contextual cue-evoked P2 responses relative to sham during expectancy formation but reduced anticipatory N1 and contingent negative variation (CNV) responses during expectancy maintenance. During pain experience, laser-evoked N1 responses showed a context-dependent pattern, with greater attenuation under uncertainty. Importantly, mediation analyses identified distinct stage-related indirect associations: stimulation-related changes in contextual P2 responses were linked to subsequent laser-evoked N1 responses, whereas changes in anticipatory CNV and anxiety were jointly associated with subsequent pain ratings. Together, these findings demonstrate that DLPFC-rTMS modulates dynamic expectancy processes across distinct stages of pain anticipation, with formation- and maintenance-related changes linked to different aspects of subsequent pain processing.

items.title: A description of legislative frameworks for mentally ill offenders found not criminally responsible across Australia and New Zealand.
items.abstract: Objective Forensic Orders (FOs) are the primary legal mechanism by which individuals found not guilty by reason of 'insanity' are diverted from criminal justice into forensic mental health care. Although grounded in shared principles, the legislations and operation of FOs vary considerably across jurisdictions. This study compares legislative frameworks governing the management of individuals found not guilty by reason of 'insanity' across Australia and New Zealand (NZ). Method We compared primary legislation governing FOs in all Australian jurisdictions and NZ. Provisions concerning the making, duration, review, variation, and transition between inpatient and community orders were extracted, interpreted, and summarised. Results Substantial interjurisdictional variation was identified in decision-making authority, detention settings, duration, review processes, and transition pathways of FOs. Despite these differences, common principles were evident, including the use of FOs for both therapeutic intervention and risk management; the imposition of conditions to support treatment and mitigate risk; and the preservation of clinical autonomy in treatment decisions. Conclusion These legislative differences have significant implications for clinical practice, procedural fairness, and transparency. Greater articulation of shared principles may support more coherent and equitable forensic mental health systems.

items.title: Delusional Ideation, Jumping to Conclusions, and Conspiracist Beliefs: An Exploratory Study in a Non-Clinical Hong Kong Sample.
items.abstract: Conspiracy beliefs have been linked to psychosis-like cognitive-perceptual traits, but less is known about whether they are associated with the jumping-to-conclusions (JTC) reasoning bias. This exploratory cross-sectional study examined whether delusional ideation and JTC were associated with conspiracist beliefs in a non-clinical convenience sample of 54 young people in Hong Kong (aged 13-26 years; mostly students). Participants completed a single-trial 60:40 beads task, the 21-item Peters et al. Delusions Inventory, and a 38-item Conspiracy Theory Questionnaire. Fewer draws to decision indicated stronger JTC. Delusional ideation was positively associated with conspiracist beliefs, r = .55, 95% CI [.33, .71], and was associated with 30% of the variance in conspiracist-belief scores. Draws to decision were not significantly correlated with conspiracist beliefs, r = .15, 95% CI [-.12, .41], or with delusional ideation, r = -.16, 95% CI [-.41, .11]. When both predictors were entered simultaneously, delusional ideation remained robustly associated with conspiracist beliefs, whereas a small positive coefficient for draws to decision (opposite in direction to the JTC hypothesis) was not robust across sensitivity analyses. Because the sample provided 80% power only for correlations of about .37 or larger, small-to-moderate associations involving JTC cannot be ruled out. The findings replicate the link between delusion-proneness and conspiracist belief but provide no evidence for an association between neutral probabilistic data gathering and conspiracist ideation. Larger preregistered studies using multiple reasoning tasks are needed.

items.title: Communicating Climate-Related Risks via Storytelling and Statistics.
items.abstract: Strategies are needed to effectively communicate the public health effects associated with climate change-amplified events, e.g., floods, wildfires, and heat waves. This review explores ways to translate complex statistics and present other critical aspects of climate change using storytelling (through narratives, exemplars, and images) to engage people and maximize comprehension and healthy behaviors. We also examine how to shape the strategy or strategies used based on audience characteristics such as adult age, numeracy, literacy, and ideology. We delineate the key psychological levers through which these strategies work-effort reduction, emotions, psychological distance, efficacy, and presence of relevant numbers-and propose a barrier-matched framework to choose communication approaches. We also illustrate key concepts with case studies. Developing long-term capacity to deliver effective messages is one step toward empowering people to act safely in response to threats, build a more resilient society, enhance quality of life, and save money and lives.

items.title: Machine psychology for language models.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a "machine psychology" for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

items.title: Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories.
items.abstract: Hugging is a ubiquitous form of social touch, yet little is known about how individual differences shape the remembrance of such experiences. In a large-scale survey (N = 15,049), we investigated whether various traits predict the likelihood of recalling a hug for its positive emotional impact and the reasons why it was remembered. Participants were recruited through promotion on public broadcasting programs (BBC) and other media. Overall, 69.5% of participants reported recalling a hug for its positive emotional impact. In regression analyses, empathy, body perception, and attachment-related anxiety were associated with a higher likelihood of such recall, whereas attachment-related avoidance was associated with a lower likelihood. Men were more likely than women to report physically arousing hugs as the most memorable. These findings suggest that hugs are predominantly remembered because they convey comfort, support, and understanding, and that individual differences shape autobiographical memories of hugging.

items.title: The Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model: Health System Implementation in Wartime Ukraine.
items.abstract: Importance The ongoing war in Ukraine has generated an unprecedented burden of psychological trauma, frequently compounded by posttraumatic stress disorder, traumatic brain injury, severe physical injury, and the psychiatric consequences of captivity among former prisoners of war. In large military conflicts, civilian hospital systems are essential for delivering trauma-informed mental health care at scale while managing patients with complex, overlapping medical and psychiatric conditions under active conflict, with limited implementation guidance. Observations This Special Communication describes the implementation and clinical workflow of the Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model, a multidisciplinary health system approach embedded in the Lviv First Medical Union in Western Ukraine to organize trauma-informed mental health care within a wartime civilian hospital. From February 24, 2022, through December 31, 2025, the Lviv First Medical Union treated more than 15 000 individuals for war-related injuries and cared for more than 400 former prisoners of war. During this period, 7538 unique individuals received psychiatric care through the Unbroken Model, including 4165 who received trauma-focused psychotherapy. The model was implemented through proactive psychiatric rounds across medical and surgical departments, structured triage into 4 clinical pathways, stabilization-first care sequencing, and longitudinal case management integrated with neurological, surgical, and rehabilitation services. This organization of care enabled early identification of trauma-related distress, continuity between medical and psychiatric treatment, and adaptive delivery of trauma-focused psychotherapies within a high-volume conflict setting. Conclusions and relevance The Unbroken Model demonstrates how trauma-informed mental health care can be delivered at scale within a civilian hospital during active conflict. Its primary innovation lies in the organization of care delivery, integrating proactive outreach, triage-driven pathways, multidisciplinary coordination, and stabilization-first sequencing into a unified, scalable framework. This approach may be applicable to conflict-affected and postconflict health systems worldwide.

items.title: Approval Matters Less When the Self Expands: Self-Expansion as a Buffer Against Low Perceived Friend Approval in Same-Gender Interracial Relationships.
items.abstract: Same-gender interracial couples often encounter unique stressors, including disapproval from friends, which can undermine relationship quality. Drawing on self-expansion theory, we tested whether engaging in novel self-expanding activities with a partner buffers against the negative effects of low perceived friend approval. At Time 1, participants ( N = 205) in same-gender interracial relationships were randomly assigned to either a self-expansion condition, in which they completed a novel activity with their partner, or a control condition, in which they were given no additional instructions. As predicted, there was a significant interaction between the self-expansion condition and friend approval at Time 1 on relationship quality at Time 2. Such that, individuals in the self-expansion condition reported higher satisfaction and commitment at Time 2, even when they perceived low levels of friend approval. These effects held when controlling for relationship quality at Time 1. Findings highlight self-expansion as a relational process that promotes resilience against social network stigma, underscoring the importance of novel, growth-oriented activities for supporting relationship well-being in same-gender interracial relationships.

items.title: Negotiating belonging and identity across the life course: A qualitative study using Social Identity Mapping with people with psychosis
items.abstract: A core part of how we understand ourselves comes from the groups we feel we belong to. Having positive, meaningful group memberships, or 'social identities', has been linked to better wellbeing in people diagnosed with psychotic disorders, yet little attention has been paid to how individuals with psychosis experience social identities and changes in belonging across the life course. Personal recovery in psychosis has been described as centred on identity and connection: it may be useful therefore to consider the experiences of people with psychosis from the perspective of the Social Identity Approach to Health (SIAH). This study used Social Identity Mapping (SIM) as the basis for semi-structured interviews (n = 28). Thematic analysis, conducted by a team drawing on wide-ranging expertise (lived experience, clinical psychiatry and social psychology), generated four themes: (1) Pre-symptom social identity conflict and non-belonging: 'I'm just something in-between'; (2) Psychosis tears identity apart: 'The map would have been blank'; (3) Social identification is both a risk and a requirement for recovery: 'Everyone wants to belong to some certain group or another'; and (4) Lack of identification with people with psychosis: 'Do I feel a part of that group? Not really, no'. This SIM-supported interview approach uncovered new insights into how people negotiate social identification before, during and after psychosis. Social identification may be a protective factor, and social identity-strengthening interventions should be evaluated as means of improving quality of life and social functioning.

items.title: Early Years Risk Factors with long-term economic consequences across key life domains: a systematic umbrella review
items.abstract: Background: The first period of life shapes later life chances, but the economic consequences accumulate across later childhood, adolescence and adulthood and fall across several policy sectors. Existing reviews typically address one risk factor at a time, or focus on a restricted outcome domain, leaving the relevant evidence scattered. This umbrella review collates review-level evidence on how early childhood exposures affect later economic outcomes. Methods The review was registered on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/szpx5/overview). Medline, APA PsycArticles, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, Education Research Complete & Psychology and Behavioural Sciences Collection databases were searched in November 2025. Systematic, rapid, scoping, narrative and umbrella reviews were eligible if they examined early childhood exposures and later outcomes with measurable consequences for education, employment, income, criminal justice involvement, quality of life, wellbeing or service costs. Reviews reporting only health status outcomes, and those focused on low- and middle-income countries, were excluded. Two authors screened and extracted independently, and quality was appraised. Findings were synthesised narratively. Results Seventy-two reviews were included, published between 2001 and 2025 and increasingly since 2021. Adverse childhood experiences and related adversity were the most frequently examined exposures, followed by childhood physical health conditions, birth and perinatal factors, and neurodevelopmental and behavioural difficulties. Early years risk factors were consistently associated with poorer later education and employment, lower income and greater criminal justice involvement. Evidence on quality of life was mixed, and service use and costs were seldom reported. Few reviews addressed publication bias. Conclusion Difficulties experienced in the early years have consequences across several later life domains and public sectors. The evidence is most consistent for education and criminal justice involvement, and thinner for quality of life, service use and costs. Reviews rarely address correlations between risk factors or the pathways connecting them to later outcomes. Modelling these pathways and evaluating interventions to address early years risks are priorities. Limitations of the review were the inclusion of studies that covered a wide range of age groups and the exclusion of health outcomes.

items.title: A Brief Need-Supportive Manipulation and Subsequent Task Performance: A Randomized Experiment
items.abstract: Within self-determination theory, basic psychological need theory proposes that social environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster autonomous motivation, engagement, well-being, and effective functioning. Yet experimental evidence that a brief need-supportive context affects subsequent behavioral performance remains limited. In a randomized experiment, psychology undergraduates (N = 121) completed two trials of a timed word-generation task used as a behavioral performance proxy. Between trials, they received an experimenter-delivered multicomponent scripted manipulation intended to support or thwart these needs or a neutral interaction, followed by a stress induction manipulation. In an analysis of covariance with HC3 standard errors, condition predicted Trial 2 performance after adjustment for Trial 1. Participants assigned to the need-supportive condition scored higher than those in the neutral control. The thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise. A brief need-supportive context may therefore carry over to performance on a subsequent task, conditional on initial performance. Because the manipulation also varied feedback, expectancy, warmth, and contact, the finding is preliminary and does not isolate need support as the operative mechanism.

items.title: Outcomes of Preregistered Studies Related to Extra-Sensory Perception, and Mind-Matter Interaction: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This review systematically examined preregistered studies on extrasensory perception (ESP) and mind-matter interaction (micropsychokinesis; i.e., micro-PK) available through October 2026. The primary aims were to evaluate their outcomes and compare the percentage of positive findings with those observed in mainstream psychology. We followed the PRISMA Guidelines. We searched major preregistration repositories, including the Open Science Framework and the Koestler Parapsychology Unit (KPU) Study Registry, and relevant meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria focused on completed studies with available preregistration and final results only for confirmatory hypotheses. A positive outcome was defined as the support of at least one confirmatory hypothesis, strictly following preregistered procedures and statistics without deviation. A total of 50 studies with a total of 60 experiments, met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of these, 17 experiments (28.3%) reported a positive outcome, and 20 confirmatory hypotheses out of 97 (20.6%) were positive.Interestingly, and contrary to some expectations, a broader comparison indicated that preregistered studies concerning ESP and PK did not necessarily exhibit a much lower proportion of confirmed hypotheses when compared with results for preregistered studies in mainstream psychology.

items.title: What artificial minds would need to remember
items.abstract: The debate over machine consciousness has been dominated by top-down approaches that extract indicator properties from theories of consciousness. Developmental cognitive psychology, which has characterized how self-related capacities are assembled in humans, has been largely absent. We propose the Autobiographical Architecture Model (AAM), a five-layer developmental framework in which embodied affective self-regulation, self-recognition, autobiographical memory, the working self, and narrative self-coherence are linked by asymmetric scaffolding. The first four, in their autonoetic components, are proposed as jointly necessary for autonoetic consciousness in Tulving’s sense, and the fifth is its elaboration into narrative identity. Current large language models show uncontrolled traces at Layers 2 and 4, fluent simulation at Layer 5, and no signature at Layers 1 and 3. AAM is an adequacy constraint on the functional roles a candidate architecture must realize, not a homology thesis. On the evidence to date, the gaps at Layers 1 and 3 are architectural, the gap at Layer 4’s source monitoring is one of training objective and readout, and neither is a matter of scale alone. The sharpest prediction concerns Layer 4. Current systems locate the passage that supports a claim when their context contains one, and AAM predicts that no four-way classification of how a representation arose is trained in or used by default. We state the dependencies component by component, derive predictions for developmental amnesia, autism, and memory ownership, position AAM against indicator-property frameworks and biological naturalism, and specify seven benchmark protocols with controls and a stated falsifier.

items.title: Abundance and species diversity of mosquitoes (Diptera, Culicidae) in endemic areas for arboviruses in the Eastern Amazon, Brazil.
items.abstract: Combating the spread of arboviruses in the Amazon relies on understanding the diversity of Culicidae, particularly potential vectors. Areas with historical records of vector occurrence provide crucial insights into the factors driving epidemic emergence. Furthermore, anthropogenic activities, such as deforestation and demographic pressure on the forest, are considered the primary drivers of new outbreaks, creating a scenario of high ecological receptivity for pathogens of public health concern. This study aimed to estimate mosquito richness and abundance in arbovirus-endemic areas within the districts of Carvão and Mazagão Velho, in the municipality of Mazagão, Amapá, Eastern Amazon. Four Culicidae sampling sites were established in each locality, utilizing CDC light traps and Human Landing Catch (HLC). Sampling campaigns began in January 2024 and concluded in December 2024, spanning both the rainy and less rainy seasons of the Amazon region. Specimens were identified at the Arthropoda Laboratory of the Federal University of Amapá. This research documented a total of 3.671 adult mosquitoes from the Culicidae family, encompassing 35 different species across 11 distinct genera. Only four genera are not considered arbovirus vectors in humans. The remaining genera include species of medical and epidemiological importance in arbovirus transmission, including species from the genera Anopheles, Aedes, Psorophora, Haemagogus, Culex, Coquillettidia and Mansonia. Environmental conditions favour high ecological receptivity for potential vectors, indicating a need for entomological surveillance near the study areas. Understanding the diversity of Culicidae reveals the importance of vector control in combating mosquito-borne pathogens in the Amazon.

items.title: Community Pharmacy-Based HIV Preexposure Prophylaxis and Nonoccupational Postexposure Prophylaxis Services in Thailand: A Mixed-Methods Study of Feasibility, Acceptability, and Service Design Requirements.
items.abstract: Preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis (nPEP) are effective HIV prevention strategies, but timely access remains challenging. In Thailand, community pharmacies may improve access, but implementation evidence is limited. This preimplementation study assessed the feasibility and implementation readiness of community pharmacy-based PrEP and nPEP services in Thailand and identified the requirements for scalable implementation. A RE-AIM-informed convergent mixed-methods study was conducted. A nationwide online survey of urban participants at increased risk of HIV acquisition from all geographic regions of Thailand (n = 452) was integrated with in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and stakeholder consultation meetings involving pharmacists, health care providers, policy stakeholders, health information system representatives, and civil society organizations. Quantitative data were analyzed using Stata, qualitative data using thematic analysis, and findings integrated through joint displays. PrEP and nPEP awareness were 76.4% and 71.9%, respectively; previous use was 57.7% and 29.9%, respectively. Preferred settings included private clinics (49.9%), public hospital-affiliated clinics (47.4%), public hospitals (36.7%), private hospitals (28.7%), and pharmacies (26.9%). If services were provided free of charge, 83.7% were willing to use pharmacies. Privacy and confidentiality concerns were the most common barriers (67.7%). These findings indicate conditional acceptability rather than demonstrated uptake of community pharmacy-based PrEP and nPEP services. Although community pharmacies were less preferred than several existing health care settings, high willingness under favorable conditions and stakeholder support suggest a potential complementary role, warranting pilot implementation and real-world evaluation.

items.title: ReLink: Reliable Deep Learning for Microscopic Motion Tracking.
items.abstract: Single-particle tracking (SPT) serves as a fundamental technique for deciphering complex microscopic dynamics in biological and physical systems by resolving trajectories of individual particles. However, linking localizations into trajectories remains challenging in realistic experiments, where crowding, blinking, and localization errors lead to linking ambiguity. Both statistical and deep-learning approaches have been explored in these conditions, yet reliable link selection that generalizes across varying data distributions remains elusive. Here, we propose ReLink, a general deep-learning framework for reliable trajectory linking in SPT. By integrating physical priors into geometric representations and leveraging confidence-based adaptive filtering at inference, ReLink enables automated selection of trustworthy linkages, thereby preserving the fidelity of downstream trajectory-based analyses. Across challenging simulated scenarios spanning broad experimental conditions and motion regimes, ReLink consistently outperforms representative statistical and deep learning-based trajectory linking methods in both edge-level and trajectory-level evaluation metrics, leading to markedly improved downstream inference on public benchmarks. We further validate ReLink on diverse real-world experiments, from free diffusion systems to crowded intracellular environments, demonstrating its practical significance for quantitative interpretation of microscopic dynamics and its promise for next-generation trustworthy and automated SPT.
